In obedience to the decrees of Urban VIII, it is declared that the contents of this biography rest on human faith alone, and there is no intention whatever of anticipating the judgment of the Church.

I am deeply grateful to the Lord for the joy he has given me in reading this book, as I am grateful to him for giving Fr. Alfredo Bellantonio the strength to complete it. I humbly believe it is a real gift for everyone. The figure of Father Bernardo Clausi is drawn with such precision, assurance and depth that the Minim wonder-worker truly comes alive, one of the key figures of “spiritual” Rome in the first half of the last century.

I had the joy of coming to know the Venerable Clausi through the ever-remembered Father Gabriel of Saint Mary Magdalen, O.C.D. († 1953), a devoted admirer of the Calabrian religious, in whom he loved to highlight the mystical martyrdom of the “Night of the spirit”, described with such power of expression, biblical sense and spiritual insight by Saint John of the Cross. For the learned Carmelite theologian, the Minim mystic was almost a living image of the “horrors” of the “terrible trial” of the Dark Night. Father Gabriel liked to stress in the Ven. Clausi the extraordinarily loving pedagogy of the God who “brings death and recalls to life”, and at the same time the response of the man who, through trials, desolation and spiritual and physical horrors, made sharper by a mysterious diabolical action, receives the infusion of divine contemplation. Finally the venerated Father Gabriel gladly dwelt on the apostolic side of Clausi’s “martyrdom”: he had undoubtedly already attained the highest transforming union with his Lord, yet the Lord, for the sake of a deep and effective radiance upon the Church, willed that he share intimately in the Son’s Passion for the Church. And Father Gabriel ardently wished the Cause of beatification to be courageously resumed, convinced that the life and experience of the great Calabrian Venerable could be a source of grace, strength and serenity in our time.

Fully convinced of these things I had learned from my venerated Father and Teacher, I urged Fr. A. Bellantonio, who already has more than one valuable biography to his credit, to undertake courageously the study of the life of Father Clausi too. Fr. Alfredo set to work with all his goodwill and, enriched by the special competence that comes from his office as Postulator of the Causes of Saints of his Order and his work as a respected Consultor to the Sacred Congregation for the Causes of Saints, he analyzed the very rich documentary holdings on our Venerable, meditated on his letters, tried to see clearly in the tangle of historical and political events in Italy and Rome at the end of the eighteenth and in the first half of the nineteenth century, and above all lingered with the insight of love over Clausi’s complex mystical life, giving us this truly remarkable book for its historical sense and theological depth, its first-hand documentation and its literary freshness. I consider it a truly successful work in every respect, a book in which seriousness of research is balanced by sobriety of exposition, truly remarkable even when it deals with the miraculous, so pervasive in the life of our Venerable. Fr. Bellantonio did not give in to the temptation to emphasize the preternatural facts: he mentioned them as far as historical honesty required, without dwelling on something that certainly has its value but does not constitute Clausi’s holiness.

For it must be said that we are in the presence of genuine holiness.

It will certainly be for the Church, and we hope soon, to say the last authoritative word on the heroic theological life of our Venerable. But a careful examination of the various “Summaria” or “Positiones” on the virtues of the Servant of God, and reflection on this biography, which rests mainly on them, give us the well-founded impression, it seems to us, of truly exceptional holiness.

Talking one day with Don Giuseppe de Luca, who was working on his monumental “Archivio della Pietà” and planning a history of spirituality, understood as pietas even in its humble and popular forms, I happened to say that, looking at nineteenth-century Rome, one could truly use, albeit with different nuances, the term “mystical invasion” that Bremond had used to characterize a well-known period in France. He was struck by this, especially when I mentioned among the group the Ven. Clausi, a son of the same southern Italy to which de Luca too belonged. Alongside Pius IX I had named Pallotti, Gaspare del Bufalo, Anna Maria Taigi, Canori Mora, Elisabetta Sanna and other Servants of God I no longer remember, and the scholar was struck, although the interest he gave, precisely in Bremond’s line, more to the literary and cultural than to the existential aspect prevented him from exploring a subject that was nonetheless very dear to him and that his pen could have brought splendidly to life.

From that distant conversation I came away with an even firmer conviction: something had to be done to make that period of grace better known. Some studies have already shed light, though partial, on this or that person, on one or another aspect of that time which I consider extraordinary. This book, within the well-defined limits the Author set himself and to which he remained faithful, provides a “tile” of considerable value for building the mosaic of faith, charity, martyrdom and joy formed by the mystery of the Church as lived by the Servants of God of nineteenth-century Rome. May this noble effort, while serving to praise God and build up the Church, hasten the longed-for hour of the glorification of one who in the last century was one of the great witnesses to the overwhelming and transforming power of God’s love in the Church of Rome.

Vincenzo Maria Clausi was a Calabrian. He was born at San Sisto dei Valdesi, near Cosenza, on 26 November 1789, to people who lived by humble work on the land. Strength of will, courage and steady, determined application to work, together with a simple, sure and very lively faith, were the riches his family gave our Venerable. He had a humble and serene boyhood, enlivened by an extraordinary love of God, since Clausi himself, near the end of his life, in the hour of his great spiritual trial, could confess: “Then I really did love the Lord!” It was a simple and joyful love, steeped in the infectious cheerfulness that would remain one of the hallmarks of Clausi’s character, something to bear in mind also in assessing the final trial correctly.

In October 1805, after trying to become an apprentice barber in his village, Vincenzo Maria entered the Minims of Saint Francis of Paola, in the founding friary at Paola itself, where he made his novitiate fervently, but without reaching profession, as he was too young.

It was while still a novice, long awaiting profession, that in 1808 he was forced by the suppression laws and the new political situation to leave the cloister. Made to serve as a soldier, he led a blameless life even then. And despite everything he dreamed of the priesthood, to which he was ordained in 1817.

In pastoral ministry in his native village until 1827, he stood out for his generous and effective apostolic zeal, the fruit of deep piety centered above all on an ardent devotion to the Most Holy Trinity, the Eucharist (he called Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament “papa”!) and Our Lady. He promoted catechesis, saw to the formation of the faithful through a serious sacramental life, and generously helped his fellow priests in neighboring villages. Mgr. Narni, Archbishop of Cosenza, rightly called him “the pearl of the diocese” and “the jewel of the diocese of Cosenza”.

But his heart was with the Minims. He knew that God wanted him in consecrated life following Christ chaste, poor and obedient, in the austere way of Saint Francis of Paola, and he did all he could to answer the call. So, after praying and insisting, on 28 September 1827 he returned as a novice to Paola, where on 17 April of the following year, with a six-month dispensation, he made his solemn profession. The humble priest, now Fr. Bernardo Maria, lived his first religious and priestly experience beside the Founder’s Sanctuary, above all in the humble yet great ministry of the sacrament of Penance, already earning a reputation as a great and enlightened spiritual director. Above all, at Paola, in the wake of grace of the Holy Founder’s spiritual presence, he became the perfect Minim whom solitude trains for communion with God, making him a true contemplative, whom consistent austerity of life plunges fully into the mystery of Christ’s Cross for the salvation of others, and whom the ardor of charity kindled in his heart makes sensitive and responsive to the needs of others, especially the poorest and most afflicted.

In November 1830, on a journey of humility and grace, he arrived in Rome at San Francesco di Paola ai Monti, which would be his friary, though obedience in charity would often take him away from it. He arrived with a reputation for holiness and miracles, astonishing those who expected a mystic’s poses and airs. Simple and cheerful, he would even resort to “clownish ways” to deflect the esteem and regard of people, who always care more for appearance than for substance. In Rome, as at Paola, he was above all a confessor. Kind and fatherly, wisely trained above all in the school of Saint Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, he guided the faithful along the path of goodness, trying to make them fall in love with the Trinity and the Eucharist through Our Lady. He read the secrets of hearts, had the strength of the saints and showed a kindness reminiscent of Saint Francis de Sales. So he was increasingly sought after, outside the friary too: the poor and the sick wanted him, taking more and more of his time, which became one of the great crosses of his life. Eaten up and devoured, he would repeatedly complain to his correspondents that he had not a minute to himself!

But with the shrewdness and resolve of the Saints he devoted himself more and more to prayer. If the minutes of the day were stolen from him, the nights bore the consequences, because prayer must have its time, or rather the love of God that burned in him must. And with prayer, penance. To the hard Minim life, to which he wished to be faithful all his life despite the dispensations granted in exceptional periods, he added the discipline; his fasting grew stricter and he allowed himself no relief. He wanted to be a man sold entirely to the Lord and to the Church. Prayer and mortification went with him on the road too. If God, through obedience, decreed that he should be a wanderer of charity, he used his apostolic journeys to pray. On the road he was inwardly recollected in God’s presence. To those who greeted him he replied kindly in a few words, at once withdrawing again into his Lord, in the grip of whose love he constantly lived.

In a humble church in Rome he had a first inner illumination together with a miracle that brought him to the feet of Gregory XVI. Then came an ecstasy with levitation in the public oratory of the Minim nuns during Mass, a prodigy followed by the irruption of the extraordinary into his life: power over demons, instantaneous cures. The “eccentricities” he resorted to in order to divert attention from himself could not keep away the crowd of those in need of soul and body who gradually besieged him at San Francesco ai Monti. He was aware of the grace God wished to communicate through him. He acted in God’s hands like an instrument that lets itself be used, generally attributing the miracles to the Most Holy Trinity, to the image of Our Lady he always carried with him, and to the faith of the devout. But he felt that God wished to make use of him. One might say that in this too he experienced the power of God’s infallible beneficent action!

But the extraordinary always frightens people. On 7 July 1831 he had to leave Rome. The Cardinal Vicar had intervened; they wanted to protect his humility, and he was sent to Paola. A brief interlude, which helped him deepen his contemplative longing. At the end of the following September his confreres in Rome elected him Superior of the friary of San Francesco ai Monti, to which he returned with simplicity and joy to resume his adventure of charity: in the confessional and in the streets, in monasteries and hospitals, among prisoners and the poor, in the City and its surroundings, he spread grace and blessing. Though he had made no special studies, he had the knowledge of God and the wisdom infused by the Spirit. Two theologians would humbly remark that Clausi had learned more by praying than they had by studying, and it was precisely in his ministry that this loving secret knowledge of God and his love was revealed, a source of light and strength for so many souls.

There was no conflict in him between active and contemplative life, no split between thought and action. He lived constantly with his Lord, becoming more and more a “living prayer”, as Saint Gregory the Great wanted apostles to be. And this prayer, while placing him in deep communion with God, opened his heart to the dimensions of God’s own heart, with a sensitivity, tenderness and readiness for others that are moving. He did not spare himself: living in the Lord’s presence, the miseries of the world and the needs of others buried him still more deeply in God, in whom he knew he would find the strength to give himself and the help to meet every need.

His cry to his “God who is charity” was joined to his longing for Paradise. While he cried: “Lord, burn, destroy, consume in me everything that displeases you,” he felt at the same time that the fire drove him to embrace ever more fully all the needs of his brothers and sisters.

But church authority intervened. At first more drastic, it limited his outings as far as possible, requiring him to go by carriage. Then gradually the requests of rich and poor forced a return to the coming and going of charity, which this lover of God lived in humility and joy, to give God to people and give people to God.

So he was repeatedly on the road, not only to Naples and Calabria, to the Marche and the Abruzzi, but as far as Turin, where Charles Albert wanted him. He was a guide and comfort, a spur to goodness, a source of miracles. In Turin he met Saint John Bosco and Blessed Eugène de Mazenod, Archbishop of Marseilles and founder of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, leaving on all the impression of a saint entirely possessed by the love of God.

In his last years, called by obedience, he had to live longer in Calabria, restoring Saint Francis’s second foundation at Paterno. It was precisely at the end of this stay in the south that he felt the violent onset of the great trial, the purifying and transfiguring martyrdom.

He returned to Rome at the end of 1847, but was to end his earthly adventure at Paola, where he died on 20 December 1849.

The life, as Fr. Bellantonio has so skillfully drawn it, combines outward events with the spiritual life in a harmonious whole that accurately reflects the Venerable’s ascent to God in the concrete setting of his eventful existence.

But this existence had a particular ending.

Fr. Bernardo Maria had repeatedly had inner trials and periods of darkness. But these were passing things. His cheerful, joyful character seemed made precisely to exclude all that smacks of darkness and the night of the spirit. Yet it was precisely in this that God asked of Clausi the supreme proof of love.

With a theologian’s assurance and a historian’s documentation, Fr. Bellantonio sets out without reticence the anguish and martyrdom of this hour of extraordinary grace in the Servant of God. It was apparently the hour of the “storm”. Clausi felt, and would repeat it in tears, that he had lost God. It is the torment of torments. And though in calmer moments he admitted that he had never committed a grave sin and had never consented “to any temptation”, he nevertheless felt that God had abandoned him for his lack of response and infidelity. And while he cried out: “Give me my God! Give me my God!”, he felt within himself turmoil, desolation, abandonment and a felt rejection on God’s part. Nor was that all. In his marvelous pedagogy of grace God allowed Satan too to raise his hand against the Venerable in a long struggle that tore him apart, consumed and exhausted him. And while he suffered diabolical harassment, voices also tormented him to drive him to despair: “Whether you act or not, it is all over for you, because you are lost.” Compared with this, what was the devil’s attempt to drown the Venerable during his last stay in Naples? “It seemed as if the whole of hell had concentrated itself against my inner being,” Fr. Bernardo Maria would confess, and his testimony is borne out by a series of terrifying facts with which the Process had to deal at length, documenting and explaining them.

This is undoubtedly something not rare in hagiography. It is a fact that cannot be doubted, especially when proved as fully and surely as in our case. Yet this fullness and certainty also prove the reaction of the Servant of God, a reaction of humility, obedience and prayer, as the witnesses note. Even in the most painful hours Clausi, despite everything and against everything, entrusted himself to the mercy of God, in whom he trusted utterly. It seems strange to those who do not know God’s ways, but so it is. When one is faced with God’s action, even through the trials we are speaking of, one notices contradictions that would seem incompatible in the same person: the sense of being abandoned by God and the search for him; inner desolation and recourse to prayer; the sense of sin and flight from sin; inner struggle and the spirit of penance; an apparent turning in on oneself and an irrepressible need to give oneself; above all, an experience of weakness, sloth, weariness and nausea together with an irrepressible, active thirst for God’s will in everything and above everything.

It would not be difficult to prove the simultaneous presence of all this in our Venerable, but this is not the place to do so. I would like to stress, however, that our Fr. Bernardo Maria never voluntarily departed, even in the smallest things, from the Lord’s will. Indeed, this proves all the more that we are in the realm of the supreme trials of the life of communion with God: the more Clausi experienced the “horrors”, as Saint John of the Cross calls them, of the “passive Night of the spirit”, the more firmly he anchored himself in the Lord, with a fidelity, simplicity and abandonment that are moving.

For it should be remembered, and it seems important to me, that together with the mystical trial and diabolical harassment the Venerable also experienced the gradual physical wasting of his body. This did not prevent him from living his painful adventure with serenity and faith.

In his early years in Rome, following his “favorite” Saint and “advocate”, Saint Philip Neri, the Ven. Clausi had given the impression of being a “stultus propter Christum”, reliving out of love and humility the experience of the early ascetics who were “fools for Christ”, the saloi. In the final trial God chose to lead him, as the Venerable put it, along a path that made some believe he had “lost his mind”. It is God’s design of grace, which through death to everything willed to make him a witness and sign of grace for many.

For, as Bellantonio rightly notes, Clausi’s martyrdom reflected the mystery of the martyrdom of the Church of his time. The Venerable himself confessed that his heart echoed the storms to which the Church was subjected. This lover of the Church, the Papacy and his brothers and sisters, by a very special vocation, precisely in the terrible years 1848-1849, lived within himself, for the Church, her own mystery. Was this not a design of grace that gives his mystical experience of suffering and love an extraordinary dimension?

We are grateful to Fr. Alfredo Bellantonio for this book. After Donadio’s first life, something serious, modern and complete was wanted. Fr. Bellantonio’s book goes beyond all our expectations. We are sure, and we pray, that it will help create a current of affection and devotion towards the great Servant of God, hastening his longed-for glorification and raising up among the People of God a host of generous people ready to follow the courageous examples of charity and generosity of the great Minim mystic.

Fr. VALENTINO MACCA di S. Maria, o.c.d.

Bernardo Clausi, witness and sign: a life open to God and to humanity.

“You will be my witnesses,” said Jesus to those who had been with him from the beginning, who had seen his public life and heard his Gospel, promising them “power from the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:8).

“He set me as a mark for them,” said the prophet sent by the Lord to communicate his message to people (Lam 3:12).

Bernardo Clausi was neither an apostle of the first hour nor a prophet with a public message, but he bore witness to Christ and his Gospel by proclaiming it with his life; he promoted the good of souls by the fruitful example of his charism and ministry, becoming himself a prophetic sign.

But why this new biography of Clausi?

Because the formal “Life” published by Donadio, in its first and second editions, has long been out of print. Because the demands of modern hagiographical scholarship required it to be critically checked. Because there are frequent requests for it from those, in Italy and abroad, among whom the Venerable Servant of God’s reputation for holiness is alive, who still await its canonical recognition, who still invoke his patronage privately and experience its power even today.

These reasons led the General Postulation of the Minims, after careful study and wide-ranging research, to undertake a work that would meet these requirements as fully as possible through serious and solid documentation.

What is required is to present the life and virtues, spirit and asceticism, charisms and service or apostolate of a man who became part of the history of the first half of the nineteenth century, not only of his native Calabria but of Rome and many other Italian cities and regions. It must therefore be a biography faithful to history, as fully documented as possible, able to withstand sound criticism, and giving exact and complete knowledge of the man of God, the outstanding religious and the priest who was a minister of grace, in his genuine response to God’s gifts, both in his personal asceticism and in the service of witness that sprang from it and in the saving care of his neighbor.

But Bernardo Clausi, precisely in his witness, answers to a particular character and mission, and is a sign of direction and conduct in both respects: a sign whose relevance is not limited to the span of his life and his times but is lasting, just as the content of his witness and his identity as a sign are of lasting relevance. For if his intense inner life of union with and conformity to Christ and his tireless apostolate correspond to his full consecration to God and to souls, in perfect openness to God’s ways and complete dependence on the hierarchy, all this unfolded within a way of life and a rule that belong to the spirit and letter of the charism of Saint Francis of Paola and his “Minimi fratres”.

To meet these requests and needs we have gone through, mostly directly in the originals, the various sources concerning our protagonist, inside and outside his family and local surroundings, at regional, national and international level. We have read and critically studied his processes and the official positions of his cause of beatification and canonization and the documents held by the Postulation, and research has been carried out in various archives to find sworn testimonies, authentic acts and documents, reports and memoranda, mostly first-hand, whose content is not generic or abstract but specific and concrete, based on how events actually unfolded. So everything has a testimonial and documentary basis from sure, authentic and valid sources, and is proved directly and, where necessary, confirmed indirectly by comparison with parallel passages and internal and external critical examination.

Not content with the outward forms and activities of our subject, we went on to study the historical, geographical, religious, social, political and economic setting, both of his ethnic origins and of the main places where Clausi’s life and mission unfolded. Moreover, to understand the roots of his various ways of behaving, we studied him not only in the immediate causes and effects of his actions but in his nature, temperament and character, in the influences of his family, religious and civil surroundings, in his vocation and charisms, and in the context of his ascetical and mystical experience and his mission. This obliged us to consult public and private sources and the works of reliable authors, particularly authoritative in these matters and specialists in various fields.

Particularly useful for establishing the chronology of his life, the location of events and the accuracy of many details, but especially his moods, intentions and physical, moral and spiritual condition, was his unpublished correspondence: a collection of about four hundred letters, arranged chronologically from 1831 to 1849, covering the whole span of his religious life from the first letter sent from the Sanctuary of Paola.

With such a wealth of material we were able to write the true and complete story of Father Bernardo Maria Clausi in this book. While meeting the requirements of a critical work through the seriousness and reliability of data checked against the sources, it also serves to spread accurate knowledge of its subject. To make this twofold purpose possible, without weighing down the main narrative with supplementary material (explanatory, supplementary, comparative, etc.) or depriving it of the necessary scholarly references, we preferred to put in footnotes everything that might interrupt the text or make it less readable, taking nothing essential away from it and indeed enriching it with equally important references, without slowing its reading.

We believe, therefore, that we have done the less demanding reader a favor by sparing them the dry maze of quotations and, in general, the mass of external critical apparatus, while keeping the scholarly character required by modern hagiography.

The specific sources and documents we used are indicated in the notes at the relevant places; below we list, with abbreviation and full title, the main archives and collections of testimonial and documentary evidence from which we drew most information.

Now that the hagiographical task is complete, may we express sincere and deep gratitude to God for allowing us, with his help and the prayers of good people, to bring to a successful conclusion a work that promised to be arduous, given the complexity of its subject, of the elements touching his story and of the different levels that make it up. We are also grateful to those who wrote about Clausi before us, each with a serious, constructive and worthy contribution of their own. We mean first of all Donadio (and with him Tornatore) for the first biography, which, apart from inevitable inaccuracies and its non-critical form, at least in its apparatus, due to the edifying style and purpose prevalent at the time, has the great merit of having introduced Clausi directly to a wide reading public, making his outstanding witness and tireless apostolate, and their charismatic dimension, appreciated. We also mean Laino, who made various corrections to the earlier work, above all in scholarly form, and brought to light contextual and documentary details concerning especially Clausi’s life before religious profession, both as a layman and as a cleric, and his native, religious, family and parish surroundings, showing the considerable importance of Clausi’s personality in the history of the Church in Italy. Heartfelt thanks also to those who with advice, suggestions and parallel research facilitated the study and its completion, and to all, especially the Superiors and Communities of the Order, who made this edition possible. May we now express the hope that this service rendered to the cause of Fr. Bernardo M. Clausi and to the many who were eager to know him better may prove worthwhile in every respect.

History, Customs, Character

Piedmontese at Guardia

The first Sunday in May at Paola Sanctuary. The Belvedere avenue swarms with pilgrims from various towns, especially in Calabria. They come to pay their respects in devotion and gratitude to Saint Francis, the Saint known all over the world by the name of his native Paola and almost unknown by his family name, d’Alessio.1

Devout people like these are found at every sanctuary of any renown. Here, however, until about ten years ago, a group in northern costume, mingling with but not lost among the others, stood out for its dignified and devout bearing and for the cut and colors of their dress. The green of the high-waisted skirts falling in wide pleats to the ankles, the white of blouses puffed at the shoulders, the black of bodices and tight sheath sleeves, and a long apron dominate the typical costume, which for the distant descendants of the Piedmontese in Calabria has now become mere folklore.

Young and old, widows and girls, their heads covered by a kind of heart-shaped miter, add to these colors that of the ribbons, different according to each one’s status, hanging from braids stiffened with raffia, and wear their hair sharply parted on the forehead.2

Geographically their town lies just over twenty kilometers from Paola, on a terrace uphill more than five hundred meters high, above the Terme Luigiane spa. Its edge is formed by a line of houses whose windows look out on the sea, as if standing guard over the Tyrrhenian below, watched over in turn by the remains of an ancient wall and tower.

Its proper name is Guardia, and its history, which is that of the original ethnic group that formed it, fairly recently added the more fitting name Piemontese.3

From the valleys “at the foot of the mountains”, Piedmont, around Pinerolo and Torre Pellice, the ancestors of these pilgrims had set out to settle in this corner of Calabria. From here their children and grandchildren in turn set out each year to renew an ancient journey of penance,4 later turned into this pilgrimage of faith and devotion. In recent years white doves fluttering between the façade of the Paola Sanctuary and the forecourt seemed to celebrate their colorful group, to welcome them and show them the way. The white doves still circle, but no longer to greet that pilgrimage, which was something of a rite.5

As for the faith and Christian practice of those original Piedmontese, at first no attention was paid to them in their hospitable new land, as they fitted fully into the Catholic worship and rite of the sparse local population, although they brought with them Waldensian leanings that some two centuries later would turn into open profession. Instead people saw in them a certain kinship of character and welcomed them warmly.

“It is generally said,” states a Calabrian writer above suspicion, Alvaro, “that Calabria is the Piedmont of southern Italy, and this common opinion probably has more than one basis, at least as regards a certain disposition of character.”6

Certainly at Guardia Piemontese the kinship is direct, as it long was in four or five other neighboring towns.

The first Piedmontese were called there, to be given some then uncultivated land,7 shortly after 1300 by one Ugo del Balzo, seneschal of Robert of Anjou and governor of the province of Calabria Citra,8 who for this purpose signed a formal contract in Turin with people from the Alpine valleys who complained that they could not find an adequate living at home.9

The newcomers must have felt at home in the south, for as their numbers grew at Guardia (some say they reached several thousand), and with them the need for space, work and livelihood, they did not stop at what was then a hamlet of Fuscaldo but swarmed from the outer terrace of the spur to the heights behind, spreading beyond the river later named after Saint Francis and settling along the arc around the coastal range known as the Catena Paolana, almost to where it meets the foothills of the Sila, between the Sauto valley and the springs of the Amato.

Montalto Uffugo and the then hamlets of Argentina, La Rocca, Vaccarizzo, San Vincenzo la Costa and San Sisto largely absorbed them as “Ultramontane” immigrants,10 together with their language, usages and customs.

The last settlement of the Piedmontese migration is precisely the one that concerns our story, as it was the birthplace and first field of priestly apostolate of Father Clausi, who left a widespread reputation for holiness there during his lifetime and even more after his death. Of him, who for his part went from Calabria as far as Piedmont, living mainly in Rome, and came back down from Piedmont, stopping again for a long stay in the center of Catholicism, to Calabria, where he closed his eyes in the land of his forebears, we shall set out the life and virtues, charisms and works, examining them, documents in hand, against the background of the times and people, places and events that form their historical context.

and at San Sisto

Following the route of the Piedmontese from Guardia along the hilly upland behind the Catena Paolana, one comes upon places corresponding to municipalities, villages and old hamlets named after Saints, following one another like a litany: San Benedetto Ullano, San Nicola, La Pietà, Santa Maria la Castagna, San Sisto, San Vincenzo la Costa, San Fili, Sant’Ianni. This is a sure sign of the Catholic piety of the descendants of the ancient Bruttians,11 but also a trace of the age-old faith and obedience to the see of Rome of the people living on this side of the broad Crati Valley, as if these places were a series of bulwarks and a line of defense against possible Saracen threats from the parallel Tyrrhenian coast. Yet it was precisely here, except for San Benedetto Ullano, already inhabited by a colony of the Greek-Albanian minority, that with the immigrants already mentioned the Waldensians entered and settled. The place that took and long kept their name, being for about two centuries one of their strongest bastions in Calabria, was precisely San Sisto, therefore called “dei Valdesi”.

Once a hamlet of Montalto Uffugo,12 south of it and east of the Luta mountains, San Sisto, today part of San Vincenzo la Costa,13 lies on one of the many slopes of the upland; behind it is the Gran Valle, the site of the great landslide that threatened the village’s survival, and at the bottom of it the Schiumalatte stream, which flows into the Ferrera.14

The successive settlements of the Ultramontanes from Piedmont, who in turn came originally from Provence and Savoy, began in the first twenty years of the fourteenth century; the later ones took place at the end of the fifteenth century.15

The Waldensians take their name from Valdès, Italianized as Valdo and only later identified by the name Peter. He was a rich merchant of Lyons, in the Dauphiné, who around 1173 converted to a life of total poverty on the apostolic model. Some followers joined him, and with them he started an ascetic movement of itinerant preaching. All who in religious fervor joined the movement were also called Waldensians. From an initial praiseworthy witness and way of life “more apostolico”, however, they moved on to independent preaching that disregarded the priesthood and the hierarchical authority of the Roman Church; indeed they often criticized and opposed it, with polemical disagreements and reformist practices, claiming a personal holiness that was self-sufficient and took the place of holy orders for exercising the corresponding functions. This damaged the unity and orthodoxy of the People of God.16

The repeated appeals of church authority were in vain, especially when the break was complete and the Waldensians allied themselves with representatives of Swiss Protestant movements of Calvinist confession. The passage from schism to formal heresy came with the acceptance of the “24 Articles” approved at the “Commune” or “Synod of Chanforan” in the Angrogna valley in the Cottian Alps on 12 September 1532. From then on, caught up in the Reformation, the Waldensians were also caught up in the wars of religion and the rigors of the Counter-Reformation.

By the middle of the fourteenth century the Alpine valleys from which the emigrants left for Calabria were already dotted with Waldensian leanings, though not with their organization, which took shape after their declared adherence to Calvinist Protestantism. So they met no opposition from the local church and civil authorities, all the more so as at that time these were private beliefs not expressed within church communion. But when, two centuries later, the Calabrian Waldensians made common cause with those of the north, and the urge to make converts in the diaspora turned into active propaganda in Calabria, the conflicts and struggles began that led to tragic outcomes.17 It is a page of history that closely concerns Clausi’s birthplace and deserves to be known in its full context.

At the request of Marco Uscegli (better known as Marchetto), sent to Geneva by the Calabrian Waldensians in 1557 to ask for preachers to instruct and organize them according to the agreements made with the Reformers, Gian Luigi Pascale was sent, who first at San Sisto and then at Guardia tried to make converts among the local Roman Catholic population. It was a mistake, as the Waldensians beyond the Alps themselves later judged, because no heed had been paid to the advice of their barba, that is, “Master” or apostle, Gillio dei Gilli, who had suggested instead that they “be extremely cautious, sell their lands and look for a safer country”, out of reach of Philip II of Spain.18

Meanwhile Pascale was captured together with Uscegli in May 1559 by the Marquis Salvatore Spinelli and imprisoned first at Fuscaldo, then at Cosenza, and then at Naples and finally to Rome, where he was condemned and burned in the square of the Castle on 16 September 1560.19

After Pascale came other preachers, among them one Marco Berardi,20 already prominent locally as political and military leader of organized brigandage, who led the revolt of the Calabrian Waldensians after the order to abjure issued by the Inquisitor Commissioner Valerio Malvicino. To put it down, the Baron of Castagneto, Duke of Montalto, attacked San Sisto in April 1561, but was killed there and his troops scattered. Later, however, on the orders of the viceroy, Pedro Afán de Ribera, Duke of Alcalá, the governor of Calabria, Marino Caracciolo, Duke of Bucchianico, who locally represented the secular arm of the Inquisition, marched with six hundred foot soldiers and a hundred horsemen against the rebel strongholds, putting the area to fire and sword. The Calabrian Waldensians of San Sisto tried to escape by fleeing into the mountains, the woods and neighboring hamlets, but many were nevertheless captured and imprisoned, and some dozens executed.21 Their property was then confiscated. The news caused an outcry, and Pope Pius IV, to halt the ruthless repression and win the survivors back to the Catholic faith, sent with full powers Archbishop Gaspare Ricciullo del Fosso, a Minim, who arrived on 14 June of that year, removed the previous Inquisitor Commissioners and succeeded in converting many through his well-known kindness and beneficial influence.22 Monsignor Ricciullo del Fosso had meanwhile called in the Jesuits Lucio Croce and Giovanni Xavier, who, besides “helping the Waldensians of San Sisto and Guardia to die as Catholics”,23 lamented that had they arrived two months earlier, or had those people been properly instructed in the past, the spread of heresy would have been avoided.24 Later the converts were at least partly restored to their property. Instruction then began for their children and for the fugitives who were converting. When a year later the new inquisitor, Fr. Nicolás Bobadilla, went there in July-August 1562,

“he found them most docile, although they had among other things reasons for resentment against the government officials who had seized their property on the pretext of heresy. He took pity on their wretched condition and did his best to relieve it.”25

Then in Rome in October 1562 Bobadilla explained to Cardinal Michele Ghislieri, the future Pope Saint Pius V, that the people of San Sisto originally had nothing to do with the religious “sect” of the Waldensians from which they were claimed to descend, although ethnically they came from the stock of the inhabitants of the same Alpine valleys. The most stubborn had already taken refuge in Geneva and in those valleys. Almost all the others became Catholics and lived peacefully in the hamlets of San Sisto and Guardia or moved to other places near Montalto.26 A few remained in Cosenza and built a small church there, but in the hamlets of San Sisto and Guardia Waldensian worship was never revived,27 nor was there any more talk of Calabrian Waldensians. The survivors were peacefully reabsorbed into the Catholic community. That their conversion was sincere, Russo observed, is proved by the fact that they never thought of resuming Waldensian worship, even when they had every freedom to do so, both under the French occupation and with the establishment of the Kingdom of Italy.

“More than two centuries would pass, and in the land of San Sisto, once so incriminated, an apostle and a saint would be born, the Venerable Bernardo Maria Clausi of the Order of Minims, wonder-worker of the nineteenth century, apostle of Rome and of Calabria.”28

Land, people and houses

Before coming to Clausi, or even as we come to him, we must first know both the conditions in which people lived, and long continued to live, in the Calabria of his time and the character of its people. This will help to place him in his local, human and social, natural and cultural setting. Judgment of a person, in fact, must not be isolated from the environment in which he is born, formed and lives. It will also be possible to grasp what he received from temperament or acquired through formation, and what he may have rejected under the influence of different convictions and wills.

Geographical location and climate, social, cultural and religious level, and political and economic conditions make up a picture of Clausi’s Calabria, that is, between the end of the eighteenth and the first half of the nineteenth century, particularly around Cosenza, which is surprising. On the one hand, the features and signs of an area that, though favored by nature, is no different from others we would call depressed: people and houses show it, and with them the life of the various towns, villages and hamlets; on the other, a more pronounced religiosity, which seeks in God, in devotion and in the Saints what it would be vain illusion to expect from people.29

Seen from any vantage point that offers a wide view, this region is a gradation of heights and colors: of rock or uncultivated hills, of earth and plants, woods, slopes and ravines rich in vegetation. At a glance its rolling landscape on a clear day takes on shades of green and pearl gray, violet and pale violet, while here and there in season the yellow tufts of flowering broom appear. The whole is dappled with moving shadows flying over plains, hills and slopes like low-flying ghosts, which however inspire no fear, since they are the light traces of even lighter clouds and give the appearance of a mirage.

Calabria is the South of Italy, the farthest peninsula of the great Italian Peninsula, and like the South of every part of the world it has southern problems, usually connected with an agricultural or mountain economy not rationally organized and with social levels that are slow to progress: it is “the south of social problems”, as Alvaro would say.30 Today, despite some lingering endemic ills, Calabria too is partly changing its face and economy, at least on the coast and in the Sila tourist resorts, thanks to new roads, daring bridges and viaducts and tunnels that greatly shorten distances. That is not everything, but in Clausi’s time and until not many years ago it suffered from the great evil and drama of isolation, both from the outside world and within its own territory: perhaps “the most isolated of the great Italian regions”.31 So it had been since the Middle Ages: a narrow peninsula with a deep life, slow to penetrate.32 Until almost the end of the last century one reached it from Naples by sea, with difficult landings on the Tyrrhenian coast, full of harborless cliffs. By land, via Salerno, Eboli, Lagonegro, Castrovillari and Cosenza, the journey even in the mid-nineteenth century was far more dangerous and tiring. Only forty years later was it shortened by a day’s train journey to Taranto, but the whole trip still took almost a week.33 The very lie of the land, mostly mountainous and rugged, did not make for easy contact between villages on the same mountain that stood back to back or with their houses always facing away from each other.34 For many, what lay on the other side or on its majestic plateaus was therefore a mystery.35 The post road reached only a few inland villages, and one had to venture along narrow tracks and mule paths where they existed, or risk tackling “new ways”, if possible, among crags and ravines lined with bushes.

But more impassable than the roads themselves were social, political and economic conditions, and these depended more than the others on people: those who held power and goods.

According to Padula, who captures the conditions of the century well, the saying he had learned as a child from his own father held true, namely:

“He who has, is; he who has not, is not; and he who has and is affirms and denies absolutely, leaving no room for appeal.”36

Of the three traditional classes, lower, middle and “galantuomini” (gentry), the least honest was generally that of the “Galantuomini”. Those who controlled everything were the so-called “Important ones”, found in Cosenza and in every town of the province. And, again according to the author from Acri,

“a secret alliance, like a rope covered in mud, bound them together”; so that with “one or two of these wretches in every municipality… the people said: The laws are useless, officials are a formality; if I do good, it does me no good unless he wishes; if I do wrong, the wrong does me no harm if he wishes: everything depends on him, and I must buy his favor…” And he observes bitterly: “This picture is as exact as a mathematical proof. How often, traveling through the towns of Calabria, so dear to us… have we doubted the existence of the soul of a people who, dividing into two silent ranks, erect and motionless as if a thousand thunderbolts had burst over them, said: There he goes, there goes the master… The people drained of money by the important ones!”37

As for political conditions, any history textbook tells of the conspiracies of secret societies, especially the Carbonari, which led to independent uprisings when they did not merge with common banditry.38 It must be recognized, however, that the underlying social, civil and economic conditions in Calabria in Clausi’s time were what today would be called a depressed area. Evidence of this depression, already serious, is a series of failures and disappointments, poverty, hard and thankless work and frequent destitution. Many old families of landowners and nobles, decimated by brigandage and war, had been forced to sell much of their feudal property cheaply. So the old barons were replaced by a few bullies in each town, allies of the important ones or themselves become such, their property defended by heavily armed guards.

Uncultivated land and idle capital, and the inertia of the new owners, created fresh poverty and discontent. The primitive and productive crafts alone, not manufacturing or industry, and the laborious, humble trades linked to them, certainly did not allow family comfort and prosperity; by increasing poverty they harmed both heads of families and public morals and peace. Then 1848 would come, and popular anger would bring ruin to all.39

To hard work and widespread poverty were added widespread illiteracy and often disastrous sanitary conditions, which encouraged epidemics and malaria; natural disasters such as earthquakes; and easy abuse and violence; so it must be agreed that indeed

“there are few parts of Italy that have known injustice better than Calabria”40 and misfortune.

This was so obvious that not infrequently, among the conspirators, albeit in unorganized forms, there were names of priests who “spoke out explicitly in favor of a new order of things that would improve the lot of the peasant masses”.41

The siting, structure and condition of dwellings, not in the cities of course, but in the villages scattered over ridges and heights, whether facing the sea or the mountains, reflected their origin in flight from the coast during the old Barbary or Saracen raids, and their perching at the foot of a fortress, tower, castle or fortified palace under a lord’s protection; or else the growth of clusters of houses and hovels around convents, old abbeys and lauras.

Where the village is larger, around the lord’s palace are the quarters for the servants, with dwellings for retainers, tenant farmers and peasants. Around the church, on whose more or less spacious forecourt the village square opens, merchants and craftsmen have their homes and shops. Then from every direction rows of houses wind down the slopes to the outskirts; clusters of hovels once improvised by nomads by birth or trade, later occupied by simple day laborers and woodcutters.

The same social order was reflected in the buildings, with roofs higher or lower according to the rights of those who lived there. Mansion-like houses for the “galantuomini”; the others rustic, mostly of one story and one room, or, for reasons of space and health, with a second floor and better room, for the rest. The latter are reached by an outside staircase leading to a small loggia or terrace, both it and the window adorned with fragrant or flowering plants. Where silk was produced as a cottage industry, once common among the women of Calabria, the rustic loft, elsewhere more carefully kept and called a mansard or attic in modern cities, even used as living space, was indispensable for the curing.42

San Sisto, like all the old hamlets of this part of Calabria, still keeps these features in the basic layout of the village, although there are changes and improvements here and there, and more than one new house has been built on modern lines, both in the arrangement of rooms and in having a loggia or roof terrace, and in the shape of a villa with a garden or flowerbeds around it. But the old center is almost unchanged, even if in the steep streets and alleys, once beaten earth or cobbles, there is now concrete paving.

The character of the people of ancient Bruttium

“I am Calabrian and have a strong will, if nothing else.”

This is what most commonly emerges from the opinion the people of Calabria have of themselves, and it is true, particularly of the people of Cosenza and the Sila foothills, who trace their roots to the patriarchal families of ancient Bruttium.

“Serious and thoughtful, sharp-witted and practical,” Alvaro called them, though he considered them “a human reserve that has yet to enter national life”.43

In truth they have now entered it with the strengths and weaknesses of their temperament, their virtues and problems, expressing all of themselves: old and new, the old tempered by the new, the new reflecting the old.

According to an old “Report” written by an apostolic Visitor for official purposes, as Isnardi relates, the Bruttian people were fierce, that is, lion-like, by nature and rough, that is, simple and rustic, in their ways. The ruggedness of their land was reflected in them. Even then the relation between people and environment held true in Calabria too. But alongside strong-willed characters, proud yet simple with the rustic simplicity that is a reserve of spontaneity and truthfulness (this must be borne in mind), here is how the Roman informant praised their more positive gifts:

“They bear hardship patiently and are frugal in food; most of them value honor. They have a great bent for arms, and with their lively wit they are capable of every good art if culture and discipline are added. Experience shows that those of them who leave their homeland, whether to see the world, to devote themselves to letters or for some other reason… in whatever other profession they take up, prove skilled and outstanding in it.”44

Yes, because they generally combine lively wit with persevering effort, especially when a certain family pride, self-interest or the family itself is at stake.

“Calabria is all in the family,” Alvaro also observed; “its strength lies in its family structure”, and “the family is its vital impulse, the field of its genius, its drama and its poetry. Children are a continuous act of faith in life, a promise, a hope, a force that must correct the individual destiny of the parents.”45

Although work or economic necessity drive many to seek employment abroad (very many from San Sisto have emigrated to America, especially Canada), family ties together with love for their homeland generally go with the Calabrian emigrant and keep him true to himself.

Also part of the character of the descendants of the Bruttian people is an innate sense of justice, a longing for it, a hunger and thirst for it. Perhaps because they are truly among the few in Italy who have most experienced oppression and violence:46 that is why they have not infrequently taken justice into their own hands. This has been shown by individuals full of violent reaction, but also by their finest champions, those of holiness. Among others one recalls Joachim of Fiore and Francis of Paola.47

The sense of justice includes the uprightness and sincerity widespread among the people. Together with the sense of family and justice, and in relation to them, the spirit of sacrifice for one’s own fulfilment and ideals, and the inner freedom that must be real and evident, are further positive features of their character.

But the Calabrian at his best, in this part of what was once Italic or Roman Calabria, shows himself in the generosity with which he gives himself to people and causes whose honesty and goodness he is convinced of. We saw this for ourselves, living at Paola Sanctuary in our adolescence and early youth and returning there several times in later life. His is a warmth expressed, if anything, in simple things, the simple means he has at hand, usually figs, chestnuts, oranges and generally the first fruits of his land, but it is a sign of warmth, respect and friendly confidence, expressed with a fullness that is moving.

For centuries this was also how the common people of Calabria approached those in power.

“However futile a propitiatory gift it may seem to us,” explains their native interpreter, “it has its effect.” If the means are primitive and the offering simple, “it speaks to what is most ancient in our hearts”.48

How much humanity there is in this! If poverty, old or recent, has accustomed him to frugality, the want he has suffered in the most ordinary things makes him warm and generous.

In this climate and setting, and with these traits of temperament and character, people lived at San Sisto and the neighboring hamlets at the end of the eighteenth century and in the nineteenth. But the harshness of the land and of living conditions was balanced by other factors, natural or acquired, that softened it and gave, despite everything, the will and joy to live. These were fostered by improved religious conditions, in which people were brought up to sobriety and a sense of limits in their various needs, to a simple and trusting Christian way of life, and to making a virtue of necessity when required.

Compare ’Ntonu

Antonio Clausi, from Rogliano,1 familiarly called compare ’Ntonu because he had stood godfather to many, belonged to the class laboring class,2 but he improved his position, becoming the trusted “massaro”3 (farm manager) of the Caracciolo family.4 Don Gaetano of that house had in fact entrusted him with farming his estates, little more than a gunshot away from the last houses of the “town of San Sisto”.5 This did not prevent him from looking after “la Bernauda”, a much smaller farm bordering the first of the plots still called “Barberia” today. He farmed it on his own account, helped by his sons as they grew up. Apart from his house, “la Bernauda” was the only property in which he had combined his share of his father’s inheritance and what his wife, Teresa Migliari, had brought as her dowry from Vaccarizzo.6 From this and his share as tenant farmer the whole family had to be supported, and a good deal was needed, since parents and children together numbered twelve. Then there were the animals to feed: a couple of sheep or goats, some hens, perhaps the donkey and the inevitable piglet, not to mention the dog and the cat. Fortunately, besides the farm work, there was work for other hands too: those of his wife, who worked wool and linen, and of the daughters, who devoted themselves to raising silkworms and working silk;7 otherwise there was a danger of the sacks staying empty; but, as everyone knows, and they knew it then,

“an empty sack does not stand upright.”

The Clausis were not rich, but neither were they extremely poor, though their fortunes had declined somewhat.8 So they did not lack the necessities, though they depended almost entirely on the seasons, which in turn depended on natural conditions and ultimately on Providence, which prepares and makes fruitful the work of human hands. Compare ’Ntonu and his family knew this, and joined devotion to faith, and imbued every household and farming activity with both and with willing effort. Antonio Clausi is in fact among the signatories of a petition to the sovereign of Naples and the Sicilies, Ferdinand IV, for the establishment of the Confraternity of the Immaculate at San Sisto, based in the little church of San Rocco in the Olmo district.9

On feast days almost all the chief heads of families of the village gathered there with the other members

“to practice there pious devotions and devout exercises.”10

The father’s example was followed by his sons, particularly Francesco Saverio, who in turn became second and first Assistant of the Confraternity, and later Prior.11 But what did Antonio Clausi most credit was his consistent fidelity to the rules of the Confraternity’s Statutes, which he too had freely proposed and approved, especially regarding knowledge and teaching of Christian doctrine, beginning, as Saint Paul teaches, with those of his own household in the faith.12

“Let each one strive to know Christian doctrine very well and teach it to others, which he can do especially at home, where he should give good example,”

the seventh rule prescribes.13

Good example in Christian teaching and practice was at home in his family. Faith and work were its title and pride, each sanctifying the other’s fervor. This explains why compare ’Ntonu had not only the times but also the children he wanted, because he wanted them just as God wants them: devout and obedient, honest, hard-working and practicing; and so he brought them up, helped by his Teresa in instructing and forming them as Christians.

Donna Maria Caracciolo’s godson

Of the children of Antonio Clausi and Teresa Migliari, the one who learned most from his parents’ teaching and example and responded to it in a superlative way, becoming the consolation and pride not only of the family but of the parish and the whole village, was the seventh, Vincenzo Maria.14 Before him came, in order, Maria Luisa, Gaetano Maria, Caterina Maria, Francesco Saverio and Domenico Maria; after him Angela Rosa, Giuseppe Luigi Saverio, Maria Giuseppa and Maria Barbara Lucia.15 Among his brothers and sisters he was one of those whom their parents had baptized the day after birth, which for him was 26 November 1789. This is confirmed by the record of his baptism on the 27th of that month16 in the parish church of Saint Michael the Archangel.17

“Children are a gift from the Lord, the fruit of the womb is his grace.”18

With this newborn the Clausi family gained not just one more man but the man who would bring it most honor.

The house where Vincenzo Maria was born is at no. 8 Via Caracciolo, halfway between the square of the same name and the parish church.19 Several generations of Clausis would live here; here too would die compare ’Ntonu, nearly seventy, on 8 June 1818,20 and twenty-nine years later, on 17 October 1847, his wife Teresa;21 meanwhile they still had many years ahead of them, in which he would follow Vincenzo Maria’s progress almost to the threshold of the priesthood, and she would go on seeing him afterwards too, and when he left to follow his vocation to religious life she would hear of his achievements in the ways of Grace and the apostolate until only two years before his death: a long road, studded with light and good works, that began at the baptismal font. Donna Maria Caracciolo had offered to be his godmother; to her, as to Don Gaetano’s various children, Vincenzo Maria, even while living far from San Sisto, would show constant gratitude and devotion.22 He was baptized by the Reverend Francesco Antonio Iantorno,23 substitute administrator during the last ten years of Abbot-Rector Don Giuseppe Archiopoli.24

Many people looked after the boy: first of all his parents, with his godmother, and as he grew into childhood and adolescence, so that he might receive more regular teaching in the first rudiments of learning, for he was clearly quick-witted and promisingly diligent, they entrusted him for the study of grammar to the Reverend Giuseppe Mazzuca.25

It must be admitted that Donna Maria Caracciolo’s godson did not disappoint expectations, for under the guidance of so many well-wishers he began to show remarkable gifts of nature and grace, humanity and supernatural spirit, virtue and charm. We shall find these gifts and achievements at their fullest, together with his physical features, described in a report by the Vicar General of the Society of the Catholic Apostolate, the Frenchman Gaume, in 1847.

“He is tall, with a quick, brisk gait and a changeable expression. His hair is black as enamel and curly; his complexion dark; his small black eyes burn like torches in their sockets; his thin lips and prominent cheekbones mark him as a true southerner. He is kind, cheerful, simple, a little careless in his dress, but attracts people by his refined behavior, by the spiritual liveliness of his words and by that unmistakable seal of holiness stamped on his whole person, of which he himself is unaware. When he goes out, everyone stops in the street to kiss his hands and commend themselves to his prayers. This happens every day, because from morning till night he is called by the sick, the afflicted and penitents. People of every class come to him, and he gives himself wholly to all.”26

Of this man, his asceticism and apostolate, his spiritual influence and reputation for holiness, we shall get to know more closely the nature, temperament and character, only sketched in a few strokes in this report. Meanwhile we follow him in his gradual growth and progress.

There is no doubt that he was a bright, devout and diligent boy, and although it is too early to discern his future progress, there was something about him that made those who had followed his upbringing at home and outside say: “You could see it…!”

What could be seen

The believing, practicing atmosphere of the family and the examples of simple, sincere devotion that came down to Vincenzo Maria, together with his first religious instruction, from his parents and older siblings took hold of the little boy’s soul, open to truth and life. Though it still held little knowledge, his inner world was peopled with God, Our Lady, the angels and the saints; with the devil too, but only to keep well away from him, whereas he entrusted himself to the others, honored them and called on them for himself and for others. Jesus and Mary, their story and their love for us drew him decidedly to everything to do with devotion, worship and religion, especially prayer, little services in church and sacred celebrations and rites. When these were over, he would go home and try to repeat them in his own way, organizing little devout celebrations in childish imitation, setting up small altars and inviting his even younger brothers and sisters to take part.27

His other special attraction was to withdraw on his own to enter more directly into that small yet great inner world. This does not mean he was a born contemplative, still less a sedentary boy; on the contrary, he was jovial and cheerful by nature, positively merry, if we are to believe the companion of his first novitiate;28 lively, then, though docile, and sociable by temperament, ready to spread joy around him. But his preference went to the things of church and spirit: a devout and thoughtful boy who did join in, organize and liven up the games of his brothers and friends, but did not lose himself in them full time; most of his time, after his first duties, he spent as described. Helping the sacristan clean the church, serving Mass and then staying on or often coming back as to the most attractive house, for the sake of Jesus present in the Sacrament and of the Virgin and Saints who seemed pleased with his little acts of devotion, took precedence over play and, without his realizing it, were his favorite delight. Home and church: this, above all, was Vincenzo Maria boy,29 and it was a pleasure for the Reverend Mazzuca to teach such a pupil, along with Christian doctrine and serving at sacred functions, what was needed for his first Eucharistic encounter and confirmation, as well as the first rudiments of schooling, and then to give him progressively more thorough knowledge and formation.

In the village they soon noticed the altar boy’s devotion and diligence in study, his fervor and progress, and were edified; they spoke of him with admiration. Besides Mazzuca, his parents appreciated him better, with a fine intuition of what he might become. But those who best knew his charity to the poor, the poor themselves and his eldest sister, who more than once witnessed clear signs of Providence supporting his charitable deeds, formed an even higher and truer idea of him.

For many years San Sisto would hand down the most striking memories of Vincenzo Maria Clausi’s devout and charitable childhood and adolescence; elsewhere he would later fill people with faith and wonder through the frequency of even more extraordinary events, but here they already knew of experiences bordering on the miraculous from his early youth. We relate two that reveal his judgment, faith and charity. People recall, among other things, as Donadio gathered from his fellow villagers, how the boy gave his still new shirt to a poor man, taking it off in a secluded spot, and the answer he gave to those at home who scolded him because an old one would have done: “It is more pleasing to God when alms are given from the best we have. If I had given a used shirt, old and worn out, how would the poor man have managed to get it washed and mended?” Another time he asked his eldest sister to give some flour to poor people so that they too could celebrate a special feast of the year with the traditional maccheroni. And when she pointed out that she could not do so without their parents noticing:

“Oh, let us think of doing the charity,” he replied; “the Lord will see to it that our parents don’t notice.”

And so it was done; and the flour remained as much as before, as if nothing had been taken.30

How constant and fervent his devotion and striving for virtue were at that time we learn from Clausi himself when, during his acute spiritual trial, afflicted by dryness, he said of that first experience:

“Then I really loved the Lord!”31

Though within the channel of ordinary Christian spirituality and holiness suited to the boy’s age and setting, nothing in him was detached from his nature and temperament. We have said he was lively, high-spirited and quick. These traits would mark his very spirituality and holiness as joyful. This is how, when necessary, he expressed or concealed virtue. Those who knew Clausi from daily life noticed this characteristic trait. That is why, before continuing his life story, since a good day shows in the morning in human lives too, we point out more explicitly the signs already present in the springtime of his life: signs not peculiar to him but corresponding, at least in part, to the character of his people.

“The Calabrian is by nature restless, eager for life, manly,” said one of them.32 “The Calabrian is either excellent or very bad,” he added.33 And he certainly knew his fellow Calabrians! “No one can fail to notice the Calabrian’s aptitude for sacrifice, for total self-giving.”34

In many cases the Calabrian’s biography can truly be reduced to renunciation: renunciation for a greater good, at least a good hoped for, anxiously, perhaps for many years. It is no accident that renunciation strengthens the capacity to endure, to love, to live. It makes one see the positive side of things, events and people; otherwise there would be no hope. And if he is also blessed with a marked aptitude for joy and can fit it to the right place and time and express it effectively, in keeping with Christian uprightness and justice, this Calabrian has an extra reserve to draw on for himself and others, and he uses it. A gift of nature and of grace!

Vincenzo Maria Clausi was perfectly in line with his fellow Calabrians in this. His cheerful nature was matched by a pleasant, witty temperament. Quick with a quip and imaginative, he had his own engaging way of putting things that made him likeable. If a certain playful style and manner suited the occasion, he seized it at the right moment, confident of the pleasant effect. His handwriting shows a tendency to enthusiasm and a good capacity for analysis and synthesis, though more synthetic than analytical: just what is needed to grasp an idea on the wing, weigh it quickly and put it into practice just as quickly. In Clausi’s life there are several episodes whose key is his cheerfulness combined with wit, which also accords with holiness, which, given the right nature and temperament, does not disdain innocent jokes and the funny side of events and things. He knew well, however, that this was not the substance of things but simply a means and a manner to be used profitably, in harmony with the fulfilment of duty and the practice of virtue. In this respect, that holy high-spiritedness, sometimes deliberately laced with rustic humor, served him to express some virtues and safeguard others.35 The evident fact of his unsparing dedication to duty, to goodness and to sacrifice is proof of his uprightness and goodness in this. Vincenzo Maria’s childhood, adolescence and early youth reveal these traits of temperament, but their fullest expression would come in his maturity.

First choice

In San Sisto, as in the Sila foothills and the Crati valley, in Clausi’s time a Calabrian boy up to the age of eight usually followed the donkey, the sheep or some other domestic animal, cane or switch in hand: it was watching, but almost play. At nine, with a hoe and shovel in his hand and a basket on his shoulder, he was already going to work: small work, though tedious and quite heavy. At fifteen, as the work grew, so did his modest earnings. At twenty, with the big hoe at work from morning to night, or with the axe cutting wood, he also earned the right to start a family of his own, provided his sisters were already married.

Whether an exception was made for Vincenzo Maria as a child we do not know; perhaps not in the early years, but at least they gave him the time needed to follow the grammar course. Then his family tried to start him in an honest trade, beginning as an apprentice in the little village barber’s shop. A “barber’s salon” in today’s sense was unthinkable in San Sisto then, but the barber’s craft was respected there and was quite often practized by women too. So the barber’s shop, in a ground-floor room or even a cellar, was the first public establishment where our young man worked, as an apprentice in the trade’s ancillary tasks. He would take up this trade again for a while when forced to return home, before and after his military service.1

But the young apprentice’s truest inspiration lay elsewhere. His perseverance in devotion and sacramental life, his equally constant docility and obedience, the innocence of his ways and a certain inclination to sacrifice, shown both in mortification and in voluntary penances, while always remaining serene and cheerful in look and manner, made him dear not only to those closest to him but to everyone. Mothers held him up as an example to their children. His long, devout recollection in church before and after Communion, following the teaching of the Reverend Don Mazzuca, together with the way he meditated and what he meditated on,2 made him an apprentice above all in prayer, and through prayer in God’s will for him.

Holiness, which in God is substance, essence, source and summit, is in human beings an invitation and a gift to which they respond by welcoming and fulfilling it, according to the Lord’s precept recalled by the Apostle:

“This is the will of God, your sanctification”;3 “be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect,” Jesus had said.4

And, as we know, in holiness too, as in everything in the order of grace, the initiative is God’s, who gives grace and love. Yet the human response is necessary in order to grow in the effort to correspond to it.

Now, that God “chose us before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love”, that he “destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace”:5 this the Lord makes us feel and almost intuit through his communication of grace. The pure and upright of heart have a subtler perception of it, almost an experience, as God pours out his grace abundantly for this purpose “with all wisdom and insight”, thus “making known to us the mystery of his will”.6

It was this will of God, ever clearer and more explicit to the young man’s heart and answering his longing for a more constant and intimate union with him, that moved Vincenzo Maria to disclose, first to the teacher and guide of his soul and then to the most trusted and respected people of the village, seeking advice and possibly support, the decisive orientation that leads from the vocation to holiness to the particular vocation of religious life and the apostolate: a fundamental orientation that aims at the heights, though clothed in the humble and docile garb of service.

Vincenzo Maria Clausi, the devout youth and model apprentice, was in the best frame of mind, the most apt to perceive and welcome God’s invitation. His attraction to devotion since childhood, his recollection and docility made him ready to listen. If aspiring to be holy and blameless in love, in its real content, is a general attraction for anyone open to inner communication, it is an irresistible attraction for those called with a special vocation to holiness. It is not merely a call to and longing for salvation but, properly speaking, to the use of the means of reaching it, those Jesus has given us and the Church points out. If to this invitation and attraction are added those bound up with the desire to become holy under a particular rule of consecrated life and to help others to become holy and be saved through the ministerial priesthood, then we have the twofold sacred vocation, religious and priestly.7 This was the vocation making its way in Clausi’s heart. For him too, in the real content of its terms, it declared itself one fine day, and Don Mazzuca was not surprised; indeed, we may well believe he had secretly hoped for it, perhaps even suggested it himself. He had gladly taken him as his pupil and treasured him as the apple of his eye, not only because he liked the willing pupil and obliging altar boy, but because he saw in him the makings of a future minister of God and pastor of souls. He must also have prayed for this, and the dream would be fully realized within a few years, through the unfathomable ways of Providence.

Vincenzo Maria longed for perfection, to become holy and help others to become holy, but within a religious institute, that of the Minims, to which he felt drawn by his devotion to their holy Founder and to his Rule, centered on asceticism and penance. The Saint of Paola and his Order were well known in Calabria.

Saint Francis of Paola is at home in Calabrian homes: he is “their” Saint, the most typical representative of their people, their almost natural patron and powerful intercessor with God. Not only every church but every home has his devotional image. The heart of every Catholic in Calabria, especially a practicing one, holds at least the ideal portrait of the Calabrian “Saint”; and before him they express their confident devotion. The centuries-long, fruitful presence of their fellow countryman in his own land, a wonder-worker in life and even more so after death, has firmly won the minds and hearts of his compatriots, who often through him anchor themselves in faith and are formed in Christian witness. Genuine in the simplicity of his thoughts, words and ways and in his Gospel asceticism; a model of trust in life’s various trials, especially in suffering; a model and saint of charity: Saint Francis of Paola, it is no exaggeration, holds a privileged place in Calabria after Jesus and Mary. It has been said that the Saint of Paola,

“a true embodiment of the Calabrian character, makes the people’s needs his own, courageously defends their right to life and dignity, raises his threatening voice and even works miracles to denounce the tyranny, misdeeds, abuses and oppression that weigh so grimly on poor, dispossessed people.”8

This is how Saint Francis of Paola is seen by his fellow Calabrians; this is how they love him, how his people preach him and follow him when they feel called to do so.9 So too our Vincenzo Maria venerated and loved him and felt invited to follow him. He was “enthusiastic in his devotion to the Blessed Virgin”, the humble “Handmaid of the Lord”, whom he felt to be his Star; and meanwhile a secret voice was calling him, after her example and that of Jesus, to become voluntarily poor, to choose a state of humility and penance and a spirit of charity that would make him resemble them more closely. But how was he to do this? And then the most humble Saint of Paola and his Institute seemed to him the right way, and they seemed to call to him from the nearby Paola coastal range: “Come!…” So he longed to join the Minims “because of his great devotion to Saint Francis of Paola, apostle of charity, as he called him, and because of his inclination to penance, which is the spirit of that Institute”.10
