Paola, by the mountain road over the Luta pass, is less than a day’s walk from San Sisto, and he had met those religious with his family on one of their devout pilgrimages to the Sanctuary. But already in nearby Montalto, the church and convent of Saint Francis spoke to him of them too: from the portrait of the Saint venerated there11 to the stairs, the portico and the square cloister that once belonged to the Minims.12 Here, more often than at Paola, being so near, the Clausis gave vent to their devotion to their fellow countryman Saint, and here Vincenzo Maria’s secret aspiration, his first choice, grew stronger in the fervor of these devout visits. He would have to speak to his parents about it, and that was the hard part, knowing how much they relied on him for the family’s livelihood; but he took courage and told them his intention.

A calculated risk

We already know that Antonio Clausi and Teresa Migliari were devout, practicing parents who cared about the Christian upbringing of their many children. Among them, at least among the sons, Vincenzo Maria enjoyed their special esteem and affection, for they were edified by his example in everything. But it was a long way from there to imagining a religious vocation for him. So when the youth confided in them and asked to follow the inner call of his life in the footsteps of the Saint of Paola, in one of the convents of his Order, they were taken aback for a moment and looked at each other questioningly, after looking more closely at him, as if to make clear to themselves what his words meant. Then, considering only human reasons whether he knew what he was asking, they appreciated his spirit but said they were against it, because of the overriding needs of the family.

The youth’s reckoning seemed to fail at the first clash. No reasons could convince them that the choice was right in the family’s situation, and to the new reasons he put forward, above all a vocation to the state of life best suited to him, for ends that had nothing natural about them but came solely from God’s grace, they replied with as many refusals, based on human considerations. They did not clearly recognize the supernatural call, God’s gift, the honor for their son and the credit to their house. And yet the signs were clear: Vincenzo Maria’s edifying Christian conduct, his preference for a life of prayer and liturgical service, his recollection and mortification, his docility towards his parents and superiors in general.13 But be that as it may, family reasons prevailed with them, the prospect of a more secure future with him at home.

In large families no one is considered surplus, since the family itself needs everyone’s labor. Resources are never enough: after the parents come the children, then the grandchildren, and so on, and not everyone leaves the family home so easily. Moreover, times were what they were, and if news of political and military events arrived late, it was easy to see that times were hard and that the signs pointed to storms ahead. Little was known in the small Calabrian village of the great French Revolution and the upheavals it had brought to Europe. Its echo, and then its ruins, were brought in 1799 by the four-month Parthenopean Republic, soon to be followed by the French invasion. Here too Bonaparte, first through his brother Joseph and then his brother-in-law Joachim Murat, would cause great trouble. But things had not yet come to that, and despite everything people tried not to imagine the worst. Why play the prophet of doom? Every cloud has another side, and things do not always go on as they began.

What mattered in practice, in Vincenzo Maria’s case, was whether the family should adapt to him or he to the family. To his parents the latter seemed certain, and to their son’s renewed pleas they reluctantly repeated their refusal, knowing it would sadden him. But the youth had good intercessors on his side and turned to them at once. His prayers to the Virgin Mary and to Jesus became more insistent. They had always heard him, especially Our Lady;14 what would it cost her now to intercede for his loved ones? An intercession bringing light together with peace and trust about his future and theirs, above all the conviction that this was not a whim or adolescent fancy but a clear and precise direction to which he felt decidedly called. The Saint of Paola was also called upon, since it was a matter of permission to enter his Order. And persistent prayer and the mediation of “intelligent and devout people”, who persuaded his parents “not to oppose their son’s vocation to wear the habit of Saint Francis of Paola”,15 won him the consent he longed for.

“Since it is God’s will,” they tell him, “go, then, in his name.”16

Grateful to God, to the Virgin and to the Saint of Paola, Vincenzo would always be grateful to his family too, right into adulthood.

“He often spoke,” they would testify, “of the goodness of his parents and the good upbringing he had received from them, for which, he said, he always thanked God.”17

But was the Order of Minims willing to consider his application? We know times were not easy for anyone and the future was uncertain in various ways, so the risk attached to new vocations concerned not only those who wished to enter the cloister but also those who admitted them. Yet, at least in this part of Calabria, times were not yet so dark as to sound the alarm. There was a risk, but it should not discourage the well-intentioned. A life consecrated to God and souls, even if it involves risk when subversive outside events occur, is and always remains, given the higher ends for which it is spent, a calculated risk.

The fervor of this aspirant to the life of the Minims and the excellent impression he made on them when Clausi went to Paola to ask for admission overcame all fears about the political, civil and religious future. The provincial superior, Fr. Benedetto Fortini,18 said he was willing to admit him to the novitiate and could begin it shortly. With a joyful heart, Vincenzo Maria went back to San Sisto, told his family, Don Mazzuca and his godmother, and set about taking leave of them, of the priests of the town, of the Caracciolo family and of the neighbors. They were happy for him, and they showed it sincerely, accompanying his departure with good wishes, some even with tears of emotion. Among them were his parents and the whole row of brothers and sisters, from the eldest to the youngest, who, though parting from him with pain and losing him to the world, knew now that his was a choice and resolve of holiness and service, and they won him for heaven. By giving him to God they gained one more title to share in his grace and blessing. God is never outdone in generosity and is faithful to his promises.

Having bundled up the most essential things, on 1 October 180519 Vincenzo Maria set out and entered the original monastery of the Minims at Paola-Santuario. Until the 10th he spent his days in retreat, in the spiritual exercises preparing for the novitiate, at the end of which, with the religious habit, he began the canonical year of probation. The superior of the local religious community was Fr. Dionisio Rocchetti, and his successive Masters were Fr. Gregorio Carbonelli and Fr. Francesco Catalano.20

Esteem for the young novice was unanimous, and so was the appreciation of his exemplary life and fervor! His edifying conduct and observance made everyone regard him as a true model.21 A fellow novice would call him without hesitation “most exemplary”22 and remarkable for an extraordinary devotion to the Virgin.23 Anyone who thought our Vincenzo Maria had lost his nature and temperament would be mistaken, however. He was and remained cheerful and jovial, sociable and quick to see and make a telling joke, but at recreation times. With his fellow novices he also took certain initiatives, which the superiors themselves, seeing his simplicity and fervent charity, allowed with a hearty smile.

“He used to keep the company cheerful,” his former fellow student Telesforo Tramontana would recount, “trying to dodge the storekeeper’s watch to take something to eat from him and give it to his companions.”

So one day he was caught on all fours using a rake to pull chestnuts out through the cat flap of the pantry.24

As the novitiate year went by, with the convincing proof he gave and the ever better-founded hope of gaining for the Order and the Church a precious member, outstanding in religious life and readiness to serve, threatening obstacles also appeared to the continuation of such a well-begun formation. The rumors of war that had seemed far from the small coastal or mountain towns of the Kingdom of Naples, especially those far from the capital, began instead to grow ever louder and more urgent. Paola too was attacked, in the front line, by Napoleon’s troops of the “Corsica” regiment under Colonel Peyri, who on 18 October 1806 launched an assault on the Tyrrhenian town, defended in vain by the governor De Michele. De Michele had retaken the garrison with irregular forces and had dug in around the cemetery near the Capuchin convent. Looting and burning followed, sparing neither places nor property. Elsewhere the war brought even sadder experiences.

The Sanctuary of Saint Francis shared the bitter fate of the defeated. Occupied and seriously damaged, it was not spared the sad events in Calabria and the Kingdom.25

In 1808 the religious barely had time to warn the parents of Clausi, who had not yet been able to make profession as he was under the canonical age,26 and those of his fellow novices, to take their sons home, since they could not guarantee, at least for the moment, their continuing in the Order, given the political suppressions that had meanwhile been introduced. Indeed, not long after, under Law no. 36 of 13 February 1807, first the Benedictine and Cistercian monasteries were suppressed, and then, on 27 August 1809, by Murat’s decree (no. 448), all the others of the various mendicant Orders and clerics, their property being taken over by the State. So by the 15th of that month the religious, including the Minims of the Paola Sanctuary, were forced to lay aside the religious habit.27

This is how Clausi would put it once he returned to the Minims.28 “He had to leave, but with unspeakable sorrow,” we are told.29 This expresses the opposite longing and explains his eagerness to return as soon as political and military conditions and the restoration of religious communities allowed.

Meanwhile his family shared his grief, seeing so abruptly interrupted the ideal he had so intensely cherished; at the same time, however, their natural family feeling revived, and they gladly welcomed him back into their midst.

The bond of blood is not extinguished by that of consecrated life in the cloister; if anything it is sublimated and purified through the supernatural, which in some way anticipates the bond that will remain between kindred in the final dwelling of the new heavens and new earth. And for a Calabrian, even one vowed to religious life and far from his natural family by circumstance or mission, it is very hard to detach his heart from his childhood home and native shore: his response to the call of blood is sharpened by distance. Clausi himself was not exempt from this, as he would show, even within a decided and undivided gift of himself to God and souls. His return home, however, did not make him change his purpose; hoping that outside events would change and bring normality, stability and peace back to the lands of southern Italy, so that he could return to the Minims, he turned his room into a religious cell, where he spent hours in prayer, especially for the needs of the Church, weeping over the persecutions she was suffering, and in constant meditation on the eternal truths.30

This reason for Clausi’s suffering and the prayer intention linked to it should be noted: they reveal the ecclesial character of his longing for perfection and, looking ahead, the angle from which his future priesthood should be seen. If at his first encounter with the desacralizing reality of a policy that subverted religious values, the fruit of a secularist philosophy, he reacted with deeper religious feeling and a spirit and asceticism that became insistent prayer for holy Mother Church, sorely tried, and an offering of expiation for her wayward children, his perseverance in seeking religious and priestly life shows the constant influence of the Church on the growth and maturing of his spiritual life and future apostolate.

So our Vincenzo Maria continued receiving the sacraments daily and kept to the Lenten regime he had begun in the convent, though not yet bound to it by vow. His strong moral support, who again became his teacher and spiritual guide, was Don Mazzuca, of whom Clausi would always show himself a grateful disciple.

“In conversation,” it is said of him, “he showed great veneration for that parish priest, his teacher, to whom he said he owed all his spiritual progress.”31

His studies too, which at least after the formal novitiate year and while waiting to reach the canonical age for vows he had already begun at the Paola Sanctuary with Fr. Fortini, lector emeritus, he continued with the Reverend Don Mazzuca.

A twofold service

The consequences of the new regime soon made themselves felt. Vincenzo Maria too reached conscription age, and in 1811 he was forced to join the ranks of the Legion of Velites,32 assigned to the squad stationed in his own village and responsible for guarding the area and the surrounding district.33 Marches, inspections, guard duty and barracks chores alternated daily. In discipline and faithfulness to his duties Clausi was esteemed and admired by his superiors no less than by his comrades. It was the time of “Yes, sir!” and snapping to attention, of prompt and faithful obedience to orders. Our recruit rose to it. They promoted him corporal and sergeant,34 but this did not make him haughty towards subordinates, nor did he take the slightest advantage of his rank. On the contrary, he was first in the hardest work and the most demanding duties; a peacemaker among quarrelers; quick to admonish, with a strong sense of military and civic honor and with loving gentleness, any comrade inclined to theft, bullying or fits of temper.35 He won over the most rebellious by taking their place at the most uncomfortable hours and tasks. With his joviality and good nature (they called him “the joy of the Company”36) and gentle persuasion, he managed to take them to church every day for a devout visit and, in every place his patrol passed through, to go and see “Papa”, as he familiarly called the Blessed Sacrament.37

So it went on until the end of the two years of service required by French military regulations.38

During these years too, with his spirit of penance and asceticism, he managed as far as possible to keep to the Minims’ Lenten penitential regime and to wear, hidden under his uniform, a small scapular and the cord of the Order.39

There are official certificates, both from the civic Captain of the Legion, Don Luigi Caracciolo,40 and from the Clerk of the justice of the peace for the Rende district, Carlo Maria Perugini,41 that Clausi took no part in any armed action and that his moral and civic conduct during his years of military service in San Sisto was excellent. His religious conduct, his regular reception of the sacraments and the example of virtue he gave in the village were attested by the Abbot-curate Don Vincenzo Stella and the curate-administrator Don Domenico Madrigano.42

Clausi’s conduct was blameless, in and out of the army, in the most fiery and turbulent years of youth. His faith and constant devotion, and his great temperance, contributed to such virtue.

These certificates would serve for Vincenzo Maria Clausi’s entry into diocesan church life after, from 1813 to 1816, with the Minims’ community at Paola not yet restored and no prospect of returning soon to the convent, he had resumed his studies and church formation, at least for the secular clergy, the only possible way to the priesthood at the time. This time his family did not object, both because they had seen once again that the inclination, direction and truest choice of his life was the priesthood, by which he set himself apart and devoted himself to the worship of God and the service of souls, and because the prospect of a priest in the house matched their hopes for him. So in July 1816, on Don Mazzuca’s advice and with the support of Abbot Stella and the curate Madrigano, who gave him excellent references, he asked the Capitular Vicar of the archdiocese of Cosenza, then vacant, for official entry into the diocesan clergy through admission to first clerical tonsure and minor orders.43 While the canonical formalities went through the bureaucratic channels, he continued his intellectual and spiritual preparation, studying theology, especially moral theology, and whatever else of church learning he would need for the sacred ministry. His teacher and practical pastoral guide was still the devout and diligent Don Mazzuca, who, pleased with his pupil, gave him the best of his mind and soul.44

After an examination and ten days of spiritual exercises, Clausi was admitted to first tonsure.45 Meanwhile the canonical banns, published from the 25th of that month, met with no objection, and the Abbot-curate Don Vincenzo Stella, together with the curate-administrator Don Domenico Madrigano, informing the Curia of Cosenza and certifying the exercises made under their direction, added:

“We know very well that he is of good life, reputation and conduct; that while he wore the clerical habit and afterwards he gave no occasion of scandal; on the contrary, he received the holy sacraments, attended church services on all feast days and gathered the children for Christian doctrine.”46

The title of support was also provided for by Clausi’s purchase, on 18 August, as his patrimony, of two wooded plots called “Lago” and “Perrupa”, formerly part of the Caracciolo estate.47

More interesting than the canonical formalities are Vincenzo Maria’s progressive preparation and the successive stages of his path to the priesthood. From the information we have we can reconstruct his course. To recapitulate, then,48 after initial study at Paola Sanctuary, between 1808 and 1811 he had continued for about two years the religious way of life abruptly interrupted there by the French invasion and the subsequent suppression of religious institutes; but he had also continued the study needed for priestly life and ministry with his first teacher Don Mazzuca. When, in 1813, after finishing military service, he was able to resume this inner preparation and study, he went back to that guide of his mind and heart. In 1816, when it was well advanced, he took the official step with the diocesan authority to be admitted to tonsure and the various orders. We have also seen that the application “for first clerical tonsure, minor orders and epistle”, as admission to the clergy, the ministries or minor orders and the subdiaconate were then called, had been sent with the supporting documents in August 1816 to the Capitular Vicar, Monsignor Vincenzo Greco, since the see had been vacant since 1 November 1806, following the death of the Archbishop of Cosenza, Mgr. Vincenzo Dentice.49

The conferral of these “orders”,50 after the candidate’s examinations on 28 August, took place, as the application itself shows, at one of the ordinations following 30 August of that year. For major orders, on the other hand, Clausi, provided with dimissorial letters from the Capitular Vicar to the Archbishop of Catanzaro, Mgr. Giovanni Francesco D’Alessandria, was ordained by him at Monteleone, now Vibo Valentia.51 The exact date of his priestly ordination, like the earlier ones, cannot be found, but it must have been before 15 January 1818, the date on which the Bishop of Catanzaro died.52 It certainly belongs to 1817, the canonical intervals having been shortened for the cleric Clausi in view of his merits and the urgent need in San Sisto for an assistant in the parish ministry.53

When he returned from his ordination, San Sisto celebrated, everyone admiring in the newly ordained Don Vincenzo the fine son of their own people, from whose sacred ministry his fellow villagers, already edified by his integrity, fervent devotion and zeal, expected much.

He was then appointed as “vice” or assistant to the local curate-administrator, whom witnesses with only indirect knowledge, including the first biographer, identify as Don Mazzuca. It should be noted, however, that at that time he did not yet hold that title and office.54 In fact Don Vincenzo M. Clausi was attached to the clergy of San Sisto, which included Don Giuseppe Mazzuca, and began his priestly ministry in the local parish of Saint Michael the Archangel. As early as June 1818, with the arrival of the new bishop of the diocese, Mgr. Domenico Narni-Mancinelli,55 he was also authorized to hear confessions, without restriction of age or sex, indeed with a dispensation from the usual age limit, in view of the excellent references given about his virtue, devotion, learning and zeal, particularly his prudence.56

The first fruits of Don Vincenzo’s apostolate, however, coincided with one of the most painful events for his family: his father’s death. Antonio Clausi, son of the late Francesco, was about seventy when, on 8 June 1818, after a hard-working life wholly devoted to the good of his family, whom he edified by his example, he closed his eyes to this world with all the comforts of religion.57 He had had the consolation of seeing Vincenzo go up to the altar as God’s minister, and his son, fulfilling a twofold duty, carried out the loving and sacred ministry of preparing him to meet the Lord and seeing to his Christian burial. As was then the custom, he was buried in the parish church itself, where Vincenzo would remain in the service of souls, a zealous priest, until 1827.58

The pearl of the diocesan clergy

If he had already edified his comrades in arms and earned a deserved reputation for virtue during his military service,1 he did so all the more as a cleric; and now, as a priest, Don Vincenzo Clausi assisted in the care of souls, giving his best through his integrity of life, deep devotion and constant zeal in the ministry of the sacraments and the word. In his plain style, full of holy unction and aimed solely at God’s glory and the good of souls, his fellow villagers listened to him with interest and profit. So did people in neighboring places too, such as Montalto and San Vincenzo la Costa and as far as Grimaldi and Paterno, where the local clergy, on whom Don Vincenzo had an effective influence, competed to secure his participation in their parish celebrations. Among simple people this is how one must preach: not in terms of human wisdom but of the science of the saints and in the apostolic manner, with a spirit steeped in Gospel virtues. If this is present and shows through, even plain, unadorned but convinced speech achieves the aim of evangelization. And Don Clausi, following the exhortation of

Saint Paul,2 had made this his own to a remarkable degree, so that the fruits in the faithful who listened to him as witness and teacher were wholly beneficial.3

Along with his words, counsel and exhortation flowed from his sincere heart, ready for devotion and open to compassion; he became comfort in sorrow, relief in distress, support for the afflicted and troubled. Always generous to the poor, he was also always ready to hurry wherever misfortune and need were most acute. In the sacramental ministry of confession, in which he followed the doctrine and practice of Saint Alphonsus Maria de’ Liguori,4 he was found to be assiduous and balanced.5 If what he received for his preaching went to the poor,6 his most constant care went to the young, the old and the sick.7 No wonder they called him the apostle of the village.8 Among his commitments, and with priority, was the inner life, for which he found the time he needed at the source of his priestly life and ministry. For this, between one ministry and another, he would withdraw to pray, in church or out in the countryside. Alone, with God alone, adoring him in the Sacrament or in spirit and truth, he would become absorbed in contemplative prayer and supplication for the very souls who were the object of his priestly care.9

Because of his virtue and the effectiveness of his apostolate, our Don Vincenzo was appointed in turn interim or temporary substitute administrator “ad tempus”,10 deputy to Don Mazzuca and his direct collaborator in the parish of Saint Michael in San Sisto. After Mazzuca’s death on 24 July 182211 he became interim administrator with Don Sicilia and, five years later, curate-administrator. Archbishop Narni, to the satisfaction of all the people of the area, saw in him the worthiest successor, in the higher interest of the salvation of souls. The office was conferred on him on 30 March 1827, when the Intendant forwarded to the archbishop the list of three candidates for the administratorship drawn up by the town council, and Don Vincenzo Maria Clausi was chosen.12 He proved equal to it, carrying out the care of souls with extraordinary zeal and self-denial.13

In the parish church the pastor saw faithfully to God’s honor and worship, preparing the people spiritually for liturgical celebrations and explaining their content of faith and grace, their rites and how to take part. He also took care of the church’s outward appearance, its cleanliness and decoration,14 but souls above all were his main concern, and he wanted them alive and adorned with grace and virtue. His first concern was that they should approach the sacraments with a properly clean conscience, and where he knew that material interests divided families or kept people cold, or worse, hostile towards one another, he worked to settle them in peace, sometimes even making good their debts with his own money.15 He became an effective peacemaker, earning by this mediation renown and prestige, gratitude and veneration. His priestly mission could truly be called a mission of the spirit and a time of the Lord’s mercy:

“to comfort all who mourn, to give them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, a song of praise instead of a faint spirit.”16

In San Sisto they regarded him as a learned and experienced priest, above all virtuous and zealous, and turned to him in every need with the greatest trust.17 But the profane must be distinguished from the sacred, and so any legal duties from the care of souls. So when, on 2 December 1825, Don Clausi was proposed as Justice of the Peace, he declined “as being engaged in the care of souls”.18 His task was to promote reconciliation at the level of pastoral care and conscience.

But there is another aspect of Clausi’s priestly ministry in his home parish from his ordination onwards. Whether assisting his predecessors or as curate, he increased devotion and Christian practice among the faithful, fostering Trinitarian, Eucharistic and Marian devotion. It is worth noting this, since it was typical both of Clausi’s own devotion and of that of his homeland.19

In San Sisto, whose painful history linked to the tragedy of the Calabrian Waldensians we know, to prevent the former “heresy” from taking root again, apart from the preventive measures ordered by church authority and the royal control over publications from countries infected by that heresy,20 the successive Abbot-Rectors or parish priests, at the direction of the archbishops of Cosenza, kept promoting catechetical instruction and both liturgical and private devotion. They took particular care of devotions already practized locally: worship of the Most Holy Trinity, depicted in the parish church of San Sisto in the traditional image of the three Divine Persons, the Father as a white-haired old man, the Son as the Risen Christ seated at his right hand and the Holy Spirit as a white dove;21 and Eucharistic life too, since the Eucharist was the center of worship, the Bread of life, the food of Catholic faith and devotion.22

After Jesus in the Sacrament, special veneration was given to Mary Most Holy, the Virgin Mother of God, as defined in faith at the Council of Ephesus, whose decrees had been approved by Pope Celestine and confirmed by the holy Pope Sixtus III, venerated there, in whose honor the Basilian monks had already dedicated the old abbey. Then, in defense of the Catholic faith and way of life, devotion to Saint Michael the Archangel had been introduced, the prince of the heavenly host, defender of the Church and of humanity against Satan and the other rebel angels. The local parish had taken its title and benefice from him.

Clausi had already been brought up in these devotions at home, since they had become part of the faith and life of San Sisto and his family were very devout.23 Now he took part in them more closely: as before in the lesser service of the altar as an altar boy, now as assistant, substitute and curate. His mind and heart were steeped in them, and would remain so in the years to come, even far from his village.24 We shall return to them, given their importance in Clausi’s spirituality.

Concrete testimony to Don Vincenzo Maria Clausi’s apostolate in San Sisto comes from Canon Scognamiglio.

“The Fathers I mentioned [Sarti and Caserta] also told me,” he testified in the beatification process, “that in his preaching the Venerable aimed especially at encouraging among the people devotion to the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, to keep the faith alive in them, and to the Blessed Virgin; one can say that he reawakened love for her in that village and revived this almost dormant devotion; and he had her invoked especially under the title so dear to him, Maria mater gratiae et misericordiae.”25

If to all this we add Don Vincenzo’s human and priestly virtues, such as his simplicity, frankness and affability, his gentleness and cheerful sociability, we can understand why he was liked by everyone even on a human level. Add to this a truly spiritual priest, concerned for the spiritual and moral good of souls and for whatever peace and well-being, if rightly used, favor spiritual progress no

“The whole district of Montalto flocked to the church of San Sisto,” reports his first biographer, a native of Morano Calabro; “they sought him out as their father, and seeing him was a feast for them.”26

He was the pastor who encouraged and supported people in need, giving away in charity even the small income the care of souls brought him. If by day his zeal was absorbed by his ministry in church and with the sick, by confessions and preaching, and by pastoral work for all who came specially to him with matters of conscience, asking for prayers, advice or help, or for mediation and protection against those about to commit abuses or real crimes, he still found time to reach the poorest in the countryside and relieve their hardships.27 With wrongdoers he had the virtue and the art of bringing them to reason.

Clausi’s pastoral successes were just as well known in Cosenza, as his fame reached it, especially in the Curia and the Seminary, beginning with Archbishop Mgr. Narni, who thought very highly of him, regarding him as “the pearl of the diocese”.28 So imagine whether he was willing to lose him. Out of the question. He refused categorically and held firm despite Don Vincenzo’s repeated requests to return to the Order of Minims.

Towards a return to the twofold vocation

Clausi’s longing to return to the Paola Sanctuary, the Minims’ motherhouse, which the French invasion and the ensuing political suppression had forced him to leave, was no secret. His family knew; the local clergy and those of the diocesan see knew, as did his fellow villagers, even if everyone preferred not to talk about it. But Don Vincenzo, though devoting himself completely to the sacred ministry and parish care, kept his old longing intact in his heart.29 Having had to cut short its canonical fulfilment so drastically under the pressure of the grave political and military upheavals of 1806 had not extinguished it. Since King Ferdinand I (formerly Ferdinand IV) had returned to the throne of Naples on 14 June 1815, he hoped to go back. Both as a cleric and as a secular priest Clausi went to Paola from time to time, out of devotion to the Saint of Calabria and of his heart, but also to find out whether and when he could move there again. Fr. Logatto describes one of these visits:

“He was a priest, and he came to the Paola Sanctuary and said the Office with us in choir, and I remember he gave a homily.”30

In fact, with Pius VII back in Rome and the Bourbon king in Naples in 1815, religious also began returning to the cloisters from which they had been scattered. The Sanctuary of Saint Francis of Paola, in the Saint’s home town, was the first convent in Calabria to reopen its doors to its rightful occupants. Granting the requests of the Minims’ provincial, Fr. Michele Mandarino, on 20 September of that year the king, through the Marquis

Tommasi, his Secretary of State and Minister for Church Affairs, decreed its reopening for worship and the restoration of the Minims’ first house,31 long before the king saw built in Naples, opposite the Royal Palace, the monumental Basilica of Saint Francis of Paola, which he had vowed in thanksgiving for his return to the capital, which he attributed to the Saint’s heavenly patronage.32

As soon as he heard the news, Clausi was overjoyed; and when he learned that they had also begun accepting vocations again, he lost no time, speaking first to his archbishop in 1820 and then, in 1822, writing to Fr. Michele Meligrana, then Superior General of the Minims,33 begging him to receive him back into the Order, since he believed this to be his vocation, both religious and priestly, under the rule of life of Saint Francis of Paola. Five or six years would have to pass, because the archbishop was not willing to lose the “pearl” of his clergy.

Fr. Meligrana, as former Provincial of Calabria and Superior of the convent of Sambiase, had come to know Clausi personally, and within the Order he had heard nothing but good of the former novice now a priest with care of souls, including the reputation for virtue and merit he had gained wherever he had exercised his ministry. So he said he was glad to give his consent, provided Don Vincenzo first obtained permission from his Ordinary in Cosenza. But the latter, asked once again by Clausi, remained firmly closed in refusal. Monsignor Narni-Mancinelli held him in very high esteem for his uncommon virtue and pastoral zeal,34 and to anyone who spoke to him about it, whether interested party or advocate, he invariably replied that he did not intend to lose that pearl, or, as he also called him, the “gem” and “jewel” of his diocese.35 The more people pressed him on the matter, the more he dug in his heels,36 except to say he would allow his return to the Minims only if he himself first had to move to another see.37 Don Vincenzo’s mother too at first pleaded with the archbishop in support of her son’s request, but with no better success.38

Don Plantedi, a witness in the ordinary process of Cosenza, describes Clausi’s frequent journeys and visits to the bishop’s palace to beg his Prelate for the permission he longed for:

“I knew the Servant of God Father Bernardo Maria Clausi personally from 1824. At that time I was porter of the Venerable Seminary of Cosenza, where he came very often to obtain from the then Archbishop, Mgr. Don Domenico Narni, permission to return to the monastery of the Order of Minims, a permission the Prelate was unwilling to grant, because he regarded him as an exemplary and hard-working priest (he was then serving as assistant administrator in the parish church of his home town), and wanted him to go on promoting God’s glory and the good of souls in his own village.”39

Though burning with the desire to put on the Minims’ habit as soon as possible, our curate had to resign himself to the will of his immediate church superior, in which he could not fail to recognize God’s will, waiting for God himself to open the way to the beloved cloister.40 And that is exactly what happened. After riper reflection, and through the mediation of his Vicar General, Mgr. Michele Bombini, later Bishop of Cassano,41 the archbishop became convinced that to go on refusing Clausi permission to follow his religious vocation in the Order he had left only by force of circumstance would mean ignoring God’s particular plan calling him back to the Minims. So he said he was willing to let him return,42 and on 5 August 1827 he granted the long-awaited permission.43 The resistance

“I cannot prevent your son from returning to the Order of Minims without opposing the will of God who calls him there; so we must resign ourselves to God’s will.”44

This was what Clausi had been waiting for, and at last, with the favor and blessing of his archbishop, who would always think well of him and to whom he would always be grateful,45 he easily found a substitute for the parish; after all, there was no lack of priests in San Sisto and the surrounding area.

“Then, commending his dear mother, now advanced in years, and his brothers and sisters to the Lord’s Providence,”46 with his Ordinary’s permission and the approval of the Superior General of the Minims, already obtained the previous year,47 he presented himself at the Paola Sanctuary to the local Vicar Corrector, Fr. Francesco Catalani,48 to be admitted again as a novice. He was received with love and joy, since Catalani and the community knew of his exemplary conduct during his first novitiate49 and of the virtues and uncommon zeal he had shown in the parish of Saint Michael in San Sisto.

It was 2 September 1827.50 Don Vincenzo Clausi was about 38 years old, with 10 years of priesthood: mature in age, at the height of his strength in ministry. That day the liturgy honored the seraphic Saint Joseph of Copertino, and he, full of fervor, kept repeating what the Church sings of this Saint:

Meanwhile he prepared for the retreat in which to make the Spiritual Exercises before the novitiate, which by tradition at the Paola Sanctuary lasted until the 28th of the month, the eve of the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel.

This long retreat in silence, recollection, prayer and meditation confirmed him in undertaking once again, officially, the trial of the Minims’ life and rule. He had never detached his heart from them, either during his military years or later as a diocesan priest with care of souls, though committed to that state and firmly resolved to persevere in it until the Order of the Saint of Paola was restored, which he hoped “would be as soon as possible”.52 He had long hoped for this return, even though regular life in the cloister would not allow him the comfort he could consider he had attained over the previous six months as curate-administrator in his village. But it was not a position of earthly well-being he sought; it was hiddenness and poverty, prayer and penance, in a way of life modelled on that of the Saint of Paola, in spirit and letter, for his own perfection and the greater benefit of others. Indeed earlier, “although outside religious life, he always kept the love and desire to return to it”;53 and this through an inner supernatural impulse that “urged him to leave a life less rigorous in privations and embrace one so strict, which he had already experienced”.54 Now that he was there, it was a return to the twofold vocation that had arisen in him in adolescence, to religious life and the priesthood, in a religious Order whose characteristic spirituality is dominated by penance: “for love of penance, in the desire for greater perfection”.55 The first to test its authenticity and fervor would be the local superior, Fr. Catalani, and the novice master, Fr. Luigi Maddalena.56

Father Bernardo Maria

The novitiate year that Clausi was about to spend at the Sanctuary in religious life, after making religion his life for thirty years, began with a new name: Bernardo Maria.1 He chose it from among the Saints most notable for Marian devotion and was allowed to take it from the very first day, together with the religious habit, on the evening of 28 September 1827.2 It would be for him a sign and a reminder of the new life as a “Minim” that he intended to live in the “fiat” of total service, after Mary’s example and under her gaze. He had turned to her with fervent prayers to obtain his archbishop’s permission, and had received it on one of her feasts. So he would always be grateful to her, and would think only of the Lord and of her, leaving them to think of him. Indeed Jesus and Mary would ever more clearly be the two loves at the center of his life. His great devotion to the Virgin, already known to his new superiors, made this natural. Time and his ministry would show how far he would emulate the holy Doctor of Clairvaux in spreading devotion to the Blessed Virgin. What Saint Bernard did chiefly through doctrine and formation in devotion, Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi would do especially through constant, trusting recourse to Mary as the Star of his life and by spreading confidence in her powerful patronage.

He was a priest, and the only corresponding ministry allowed him during the novitiate was the daily celebration of Holy Mass. Yet it was precisely here that the best of his Christ-centered devotion found expression. Jesus in the Eucharist, in the offering of the renewed sacrifice, concentrated and focused him to the utmost. “His” Mass was that of a minister full of faith and fervor, held in check by discreet devotion, when it did not turn into ecstasy or silent Eucharistic dialogue, shown in a face lit by a flush that was not a natural reflex. The religious noticed it, and so did the faithful who attended, who sensed the difference in inwardness compared with other celebrants and were confirmed in the reputation that had reached them of the holy curate of San Sisto, who had come to the Paola Sanctuary to become still holier under the Minims’ rule of life.

Most exact in observing the regular discipline, apart from the common duties and those of the novitiate, our novice gave ample room to recollection and prayer: the very things that in the world had been his voluntary refuge, out of a need for union with God and inner strength for the benefit of his sacred ministry as well as his own sanctification, here found better opportunities, by day and by night, at night even more than by day: in choir, in church and in his own cell, where he could give himself fully to the adoration and love of the adorable Trinity.

To prayer Br. Bernardo Maria added severe asceticism, physical too, with frequent mortifications and harsh disciplines.3 Who would have thought it? Yet he was the most warm-hearted and cheerful of all, letting nothing show of the severity he used with himself. The ascetic must be open to the joy of salvation, and Clausi’s cheerful nature, which gave a vein of joy to his behavior, made this easier. But his long ascetic training in the world under Don Mazzuca, his teacher from early childhood and later also his confessor and spiritual director, made him follow, as the criterion and principle of sound asceticism, the clear Gospel warning: “When you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that your fasting may be seen not by others but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father who sees in secret will reward you.”4 We shall find this to be his secret rule of conduct in practice, protecting not only the virtue of penance but also, and especially, humility, all the more as the reputation for holiness grew more rooted and widespread. But the long days of weeping would come, when the Lord himself would test his virtue and fidelity to the utmost, and the Gospel warning would come literally true for Fr. Bernardo: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.”5 It would be a mystical fast, sharply purifying and at the same time leading to greater perfection. Meanwhile, what a man prudently and discreetly hides out of humility God brings to light for edification and example. His fellow novices were the first witnesses, and there is good reason to believe they were also the first to spread the word. With the novices, the fathers and brothers, and no less those who came up to the Sanctuary,6 admired his deep spirit of devotion, his integrity of life and religious discipline.7

“The books of our Order,” the Vicar General would attest, “record that he was an exemplary novice.”8

If in his first novitiate the young Clausi had been an example and a model, in this second one, matured by age and far greater experience, backed by a level of virtue no longer that of a beginner and sustained both in inner life and in thorough asceticism, he was certainly no less so. Fr. Luigi Martini, whom we shall often meet with Clausi, would testify:

“From the time when I was a student in Rome, at the College of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti, I constantly heard it said that the Servant of God during his novitiate never did anything contrary to the novitiate Rule; on the contrary, he was an edifying example to the other novices, and throughout that time he always fulfilled exactly all the obligations of his state.”

And of this second novitiate in particular he also testifies that

“he was an uncommon example to his companions, to the religious and to all the people.”9

Such intense and exemplary preparation for his coming profession, in a novice who had already spent, with fully satisfactory results, not just one year but more than two of edifying discipline in that first novitiate begun in 1805, which he had not completed with vows because he was under age and because of the well-known political and military events that sent him back to the world against his will, would be a valid argument for asking the Holy See to reduce f3ltf? his novitiate by six months. His superiors wanted it, and the community unanimously expressed the same wish.10 He was a priest far advanced in virtue, especially in prudence and in the exercise of the sacred ministry over the previous ten years in the diocese, and confessors were needed at the Sanctuary, where pilgrims came in large numbers. This was one more reason for a formal petition, all the more since the candidate fully deserved it, for

“by a special vocation he has embraced the religious state of the Order,” the petition specifies, “despite the austerity of the perpetual Lenten life… A priest for eleven years, aged thirty-eight, of excellent morals and an approved confessor…”,11 “recommended for his outstanding gifts of soul and virtue not only by the petitioner, Superior of the Paola Sanctuary, but also by our Most Reverend Father General.”12

So without waiting for 29 September, the traditional date for professions at the Paola motherhouse, on 17 April 1828 Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi, after a regular course of Spiritual Exercises spent in strict recollection and fervor,13 consecrated himself for ever under the Minims’ Rule, making the vows of obedience, chastity, poverty and Lenten life into the hands of the Provincial, Fr. Bernardo M. Marsicani. At that time this was the only profession, perpetual and solemn.14 Attendance was spontaneous and large, including the faithful, who knew of his reputation for holiness.15 A clear sign of the newly professed’s unspeakable joy at pronouncing his holy vows and knowing that by this act he had definitively entered the Minim family and the life he had so long desired was the quiet weeping that followed the formula he pronounced with emotion. Then Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi prostrated himself to kiss the ground, thanked his religious brothers for admitting him to the Order and exclaimed with emotion: “Haec requies mea, in saeculum saeculi” (This is my resting place for ever).16

Life and ministry at Paola

As a professed religious and priest of the Minims, Fr. Clausi began his ministry at the Paola Sanctuary.

The role of shrines, before being centers of special veneration for one or another mystery of our holy Religion, or for some title of Our Lady or a Saint whose memory lives on in the record of an exemplary life, of the places where he lived or of his tomb and notable relics, is to be oases of the spirit. What draws people there is essentially the need for inwardness, sacramental life, a more intimate encounter with God, rest for the soul and a review of one’s life or renewal of conduct, if not actual conversion and reconciliation, in the spirit of the mystery venerated there, or of the Virgin or Saint particularly celebrated there. It is therefore extremely important that priests serving in shrines be of exemplary virtue and have adequate learning and zeal for the salvation of souls.

Fr. Bernardo had these qualities and already had considerable experience in pastoral ministry. We also know that his reputation had spread around Cosenza, together with the news that he had entered the Order of Saint Francis of Paola and was living at the Paola Sanctuary. The name of Paola, ever since its most illustrious son, Francesco d’Alessio, took his name from it, had spread throughout the world together with the fame of his heroic virtues and his miracles. So in the minds and hearts of the Saint’s devotees it merges with the Sanctuary that gives it prestige, and Paola sees itself honored by its Saint.17

Here for centuries pilgrims have come who, whether in Francis’s lifetime or after his death and beatification, understood him to be among the Blessed, had some need of the soul to bring to him. Calabria, and not only Calabria, pours in here, especially on the now traditional days of the Paola festivities at the beginning of May. But at any time of year individual pilgrims or groups climb to the Sanctuary for a bath of devotion and Paolan or “Minim” spirituality. We are in the Minims’ motherhouse, founded by Saint Francis on the site of his first hermitage,18 and the places associated with him bear eloquent witness to his long vigils in prayer and frequent ecstasies, to his spiritual and austere life, hard-working, humble and penitent, and to his acts of charity, very often crowned by miracles.

The convent and church of Saint Francis have a history woven of events, from the building of the sacred edifices to their enlargements and more or less radical restorations; from countless celebrations to religious renowned for virtue and learning, lined up as in a portrait gallery;19 from visitors and pilgrims to distinguished benefactors, whose memory is now part of that of the Saint and his Sanctuary.20

The mystical feeling of the surrounding countryside, the solemn silence from evening to morning, broken only by the murmur of the stream below, a distant bark or the wind in the woods, when it blows, rustling and whistling in waves, also takes hold of the pilgrim’s heart, disposing him for the encounter with grace renewed there. But it is not only the mysticism of nature and the charm of places full of history and grateful devotion; it is the living presence of a spirit and a message that make one reflect and move one to an inner sense of charity, humility and self-denial, for a renewal of outlook and conduct which, after the Saint’s wonderful example, is the true “Grace” of Paola.

Here, then, those who came to Saint Francis found Fr. Bernardo, the new “Minim”, a zealous minister of the Sanctuary. The esteem and trust he inspired, though he was so reserved and shunned any outward show, doubled the pilgrims’ reason and interest in coming. To his already known reputation for holiness was added his welcoming priestly zeal in presenting the message of Saint Francis of Paola’s virtues to devout visitors and in taking up their prayers and vows; he broke for them the bread of the word, of counsel, comfort and salutary warning, and joined to it his own prayerful mediation. And the help of prayer was often an effective intercession.

Such progress in holiness and such an effective apostolate helped spread his reputation throughout Calabria and beyond, in every direction, as far as Rome and further.21

Paola is the most complete place to absorb the spirit of Saint Francis. Everything there speaks of him, of his life, his charism and holiness. His work shows through the overhanging rocks and the memories, the fruit of a sublime inner life, both contemplative and apostolic, placed wholly at the disposal of God and souls. The “desert” and the “cave of penance”, the kiln of “Martinello” brought back to life and the “cucchiarella” spring, the “stones of the miracle”, the “cave of catechesis” and the first hermitage, the Saint’s cell and the whole complex of buildings of which every stone, one might say, recalls something he did; even the natural surroundings, mountains, stream and woods, with the sea in the background, give voice and echo to a teaching that our Fr. Bernardo took as the inspiration and pattern of the authentic spirit of a religious “Minim”: utterly humble, used to sacrifice, warmly available and sharing in charity.

But two particular traits of the spirit and life of the Founder from Paola were copied in a special way by Fr. Clausi: the man of prayer and the penitent. “He would spend hours prostrate on the floor of the cell once occupied by his Father Saint Francis,” we are told,22 renewing his vigils and disciplines, or else in the choir, for the same purpose.23 Returning to the works of the sacred ministry, he brought to them a store of humility and fervent charity proper to those who give themselves to God with all their heart, all their soul and all their strength. And he bore God’s sign in the manifestation of supernatural power, of which he was made witness and instrument. This was the steady growth of grace and holiness that filled his spirit more and more. Already here and at this time, in fact, Fr. Bernardo showed the virtues that would so adorn him in later years, setting him above common esteem,24 and displayed more than one charism. And there were more and more events that, while bringing renown to the Sanctuary, spread Clausi’s name as the most sought-after priest.

His dedication to the service of God and souls stood out for holiness of life and zeal in the sacred ministry, the defining features of his ascetic striving for religious perfection and of his apostolate, which set him apart even among his own brethren.

It is well known that the restoration of religious houses is not always matched by renewed fervor in discipline, especially among members whom political and military events had earlier removed from the cloister and accustomed to different habits. This called for closer vigilance on the part of both church and civil authorities, as the exceptional times required. So there were visitations and reports on discipline. One such “visitation” to the Paola Sanctuary was made in 1830 by the former Superior General, Fr. Michele Meligrana, in his new capacity as Apostolic Delegate.25 Years before, during a similar canonical visitation as General to the convent of Polistena, he had heard the priest Don Vincenzo Clausi spoken of with great esteem as a former Minim novice at the time when the Orders were suppressed and the convents closed.26 He himself had given him permission to return, knowing that he was highly regarded for his virtue and fervent vocation to the Order. The visit to Paola, however, as far as Clausi was concerned, would be the occasion for God, who was guiding him, to reveal a wider providential plan. While celebrating Holy Mass, Fr. Meligrana unexpectedly witnessed a miraculous event involving Fr. Bernardo, who was in the small choir behind the altar, unaware that he was being watched.

This unexpected and surprising direct observation led Fr. Meligrana, who already knew of other miraculous events attributed to Clausi, to test the real degree of his virtue: whether he was truly so dear to God as to draw his favor and gifts of grace. The keystone of religious virtue is humility, detachment and prompt, persevering obedience combined. So after Mass he called him and ordered him to leave the Paola Sanctuary and go to Reggio Calabria, where he would find instructions about his new residence. Fr. Clausi left at once in obedience.27

He made the long, tiring journey on foot.28 We may imagine him thinking of the Holy Founder’s journey to the shore at Catona and feeling in his heart that he was following in his footsteps.29 At the Reggio post office, as instructed, he did find a letter telling him to move to the convent of S. Maria della Stella in Naples. So he set out on the new journey, back the way he had come.30 There, however, he found another letter with the formal obedience assigning him to the convent of Saint Francis of Paola in Rome.31 He stopped three or four days in all, just long enough to recover from the journeys already made, and set off again.

What the miracle behind this test and transfer was is not specified in the source, since it comes from an indirect witness to whom it was not revealed, the Reverend Felice De Gennaro, who testified under oath:

“I remember hearing in Naples from the General Meligrana that the Servant of God, shortly after his profession, was sent from the convent of Paola to that of Rome, namely ai Monti, and he told me the following. He, that is the General, was saying Mass one day at the high altar of the church in Paola, and since through this pierced altar the celebrating priest could see into the choir on the other side, behind the altar, he noticed that the Servant of God, who was then in the choir, worked a miracle at that moment. After Mass, for this reason, as the General told me, he gave him a verbal obedience to go to Reggio Calabria, where at the post office, etc. In Naples, after two days, he received from the same General the obedience for Rome… His mind was cheerful and calm… What miracle he had worked I was not told, nor what purpose the General had in acting thus.”32

Fr. Bernardo’s exemplary presence at the Paola Sanctuary over the previous three years was genuinely recognized by the bishop of the diocese. The Archbishop of Cosenza, who had known and appreciated him well as a diocesan priest, wrote in his half-yearly report on the restored convents, six of them by the end of August 1830, including the “Paolotti of Paola”: “As for the Paolotti of Paola, I am of the opinion that the whole community should be changed, except Fr. Assisi and Fr. Clausi.”33

The Vicar General for the Italian Provinces, Fr. Bernardo Marsicani, shared the bishop’s esteem and opinion. On the 31st of that same month he had petitioned the Holy Father, as he intended to entrust Fr. Clausi with the office of Superior of the Paola Sanctuary, but since he did not yet have the three years of profession required by the Rule for that office, an indult from the Holy See was needed.34 The indult was granted on 6 September 1830 by rescript of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, “non obstantibus Constitutionibus Ordinis”; but nothing came of it, because meanwhile the Apostolic Delegate’s transfer had intervened, to make better use of Clausi at the center of Christendom. In Rome this was welcomed with full approval.

The Minims’ College and the National Church of the Calabrians

Rome has a unique character and attraction for believers, whether lay faithful, priests or religious. All look to it as the center of Catholic unity, almost the geographical capital of God’s Kingdom among men. A visit to the “Memorials” of the Apostles and the countless witnesses of Christian Rome, a devout encounter with the Vicar of Christ, who has his visible see and representation here in the Successor of Peter, have always been among the most heartfelt aspirations of millions, perhaps a long-cherished dream they hope will come true. Today the fascination and love of this privileged city continue, whatever other circumstances may apply; for many, indeed, coming here is no longer an extraordinary event, and the soul that arrives is inwardly disposed to receive a gift, almost a visit from the invisible Christ who passes in his Vicar and knocks to enter as Lord of Catholic faith, charity and unity.

A century and a half ago, for a man from Calabria, even a priest and religious, it was not so easy or safe. Yet Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi was sent there without any expectation on his part, and he arrived preceded by a reputation that spread as if by magic: a reputation certainly not exceeding his merits, for his outstanding virtue had merit enough, nor limited to them, but extending to the signs with which God goes before and accompanies his faithful minister.1 In Rome they did not yet know him personally, but people spoke of him and his virtues with edification.

“They said a Saint was coming,” Canon Carlo Valletta reports, “and before he reached Rome, when he arrived at Genzano, where I happened to be on business, the people were so moved that almost the whole town went out to meet him… and the archpriest, a man of holy life who died with a reputation for holiness, was so comforted in spirit that for several days he spoke of nothing but this Servant of God.”2

They saw him as the awaited one whom people prefer to go out and meet, because the heart needs to see, hear and touch the witnesses of the Word that is life. Something like what had happened with Saint Francis of Paola on his journeys and successive stays.3

So the final destination of Clausi’s first transfer was Rome, and his residence the Minims’ Convent-College with the adjoining church of Saint Francis of Paola, in the Monti district.

Up here, a little below the present church, in imperial times, when the Roman Forum was no longer the usual place for trials, stood the city’s Tribunal, of which Martial speaks.4 Here too, in underground rooms, Christians awaiting trial were imprisoned and not infrequently tortured to make them renounce their faith.5 From here, finally, after the Prefect had pronounced sentence, the sad procession of those condemned to death set out and was led along the path corresponding to today’s Via in Selci to the usual place of execution on the Esquiline, roughly between today’s Saint Mary Major, Via Napoleone III and Piazza Vittorio.6 Here too, in the Fourth Region of imperial times, but in an even older period, that of Servius, near the vicus patricius and the clivus suburranus, lay the infamous vicus sceleratus where, according to tradition, the murder took place of the husband and sister of the ambitious Tullia and of Servius Tullius’s usurper, Tarquin the Proud, as recorded by Livy.7

Rome in this part of the city, as far as the Castro Pretorio or “Macao”, now home to the new National Library, was still far from having the grid of streets and buildings showing the influence of Piedmontese town planning. Here both the Suburra and the Polveriera area, on either side of San Francesco da Paola ai Monti, had the character of “vanished Rome”, with street names still surviving, Via del Boschetto (copse), dei Serpenti (serpents), degli Zingari (gypsies) and di Caprareccia (goat pen), that well express its rustic, working-class look, alongside others, Eudossiana, dei Frangipane, delle Sette Sale, that recall later owners and developments. Houses and hovels around grander ones formed sunburnt gray patches among the greenery, or rows of plastered stone with tiled roofs.

Convent and church, together with the bell tower, the only example in Rome of a genuine medieval tower used as a belfry, form a block surrounded by the remains of three old gardens that once made this hill so pleasant. From the front of the buildings the ground slopes away with narrow streets leading from the square: one towards the Colosseum, another towards the “Madonna dei Monti”, and another that turns down a few steps and forks towards the Salita dei Borgia and Via in Selci. Two centuries earlier, however, the present complex did not yet exist, only the old palace or villa Cesarini onto which it is grafted.9

It is worth turning back to a page in the history of the old complex. It was the Calabrian priest Don Giovanni Pizzullo,10 formerly chaplain at the Santi Dodici Apostoli and later canon of San Lorenzo in Damaso, who wanted it built in honor of the Saint of Calabria and to strengthen and represent the Minims in Rome. His gratitude to these religious, who had cared for his early education in the town of Regina, and his devotion to the Saint moved him to devote a large part of his property and income to what became in effect the “national” Church of the Calabrians and the study Convent-College of the Minim religious of Calabria Citra, the Cosenza area.11

In a will drawn up by the notary Ottavio Capogallo on 10 January 1621, Pizzullo had made the Minims of the convent of S. Andrea delle Fratte12 his universal heirs, on condition that they founded a College there for student fathers of the Order of Calabrian nationality, and that they acquired a church or “a site or cottage” on which to build a new church “dedicated to Saint Francis of Paola”.13 In return he asked, besides various suffrages, to be buried provisionally in Sant’Andrea delle Fratte and later transferred to the new church.14 Then, as to the distribution of his property:

“I leave two thousand scudi in coin to the Reverend Fathers of Saint Francis of Paola of the Order of Minims living in the town of Regina, my homeland,” he specified. “In all and each of my other goods, movable, immovable and livestock [etc.] I institute and leave, and in my own hand here name and write as my universal heirs, the Reverend Fathers of the Order of Minims of the convent of S. Andrea delle Fratte in Rome… on condition, however, and with the obligation and charge of spending at least six thousand scudi in coin to acquire a church in Rome, or a site… [etc., as reported] and a hospice or College of the said Order for the Calabrian nation…”15

But Pizzullo was impatient to see the work done, and two years later, on 4 February 1623, he bought the Cesarini Dukes of Civitanova’s palace or “Villa”, with its outbuildings and adjoining gardens, including

The church and College had their greatest splendor in the second half of the seventeenth and throughout the eighteenth century, with religious renowned for virtue and learning working there, some in the parish, others in studies.29 Pastoral care, religious discipline and formation flourished. So it remained until Rome was occupied by French troops, Pius VI was captured and exiled, and Bonaparte carried out the first political suppression of male religious institutes, leaving only the parish ministry.30 But this too lasted only a few more years, because in 1824 Pope Leo XII, through the Constitution “Super universam”, and on his behalf the new Cardinal Vicar Placido Zurla, revised the pastoral plan for Rome, including a redistribution of parishes.31 Some were suppressed, others moved, among them the parish of Saint Francis of Paola. Its font was moved to Saint Mary Major, and the old parish boundaries were changed, its territory and population being divided between the parish of San Martino ai Monti and the new parish of the nearby Madonna dei Monti.32

Exactly two centuries had passed, during which the Calabrian Minims had lavished pastoral ministry there with direct parish jurisdiction.

First stay in Rome

With the arrival of Fr. Bernardo Maria Clausi at “San Francesco di Paola ai Monti” on 9 November 183033 a new era began for the national Church and College of the Calabrians in Rome. His arrival, of the humblest kind,34 was preceded, as we have said, by the reputation of his outstanding virtues and the charisms accompanying him.35 The religious community was happy to count him among its members, from the first in rank, the Vicar General Fr. Marsicani, to the simple Br. Lorenzo Muzzillo.36 The latter, known in Roman circles for his remarkable devotion and virtue and himself sought out by people who wanted his prayers or advice, told those who came to him that a holy father was coming among them: “a holy father who works miracles”, he confided, for example, to one Ferdinando Bellini. When Fr. Bernardo arrived and, with his “simple and cheerful” manner, gave no sign of being “that holy father who works miracles”, having instead a very personal, easy way of hiding his virtues, the eager devotee and friend asked:

“But Brother Lorenzo, is this really the holy friar who works miracles?” And Brother Lorenzo replied: “Ferdinando, you’ll see!”37

The description of him made on 28 July of the following year gives a precise idea of how Clausi appeared to the Romans when he first arrived in the City.

“He is 32 years old [sic], of medium height, neither thin nor fat; of cheerful temperament, affable with everyone and very gracious. His great qualities are supreme humility and blind obedience. He is especially devoted to the Most Holy Trinity. Although he does not know people, he calls them by name.”38

Further details about the man and holy religious come from Canon Valletta.

“Beneath certain curious appearances very typical of his province of Calabria lay a depth of extraordinary virtue, which God bestowed on him (sic), protecting him in wonderful ways.”39

The cornerstones of this virtue, according to Valletta, were that he

“based his conduct on two great principles of our Religion: the folly of the Cross, so that he often observed Saint Paul’s ‘Nos stulti propter Christum’ to the letter; and secondly, he walked in a special way in the presence of God, by which he guided himself to receive light and act in countless cases.”40

Nor did his manner contradict this virtue, since

“for all that, even in his jokes he spoke very well of God”, and “although he used those ways of his, somewhat comical… his words were measured, modest and always aimed at giving good instruction, so that those who listened to him were greatly edified.”41

Meanwhile people began asking Fr. Bernardo to hear their confessions, and he prepared, more by prayer than by study, to take the examinations required to be licensed. This was the wish of his immediate Major Superior, Fr. Marsicani, and the canonical practice of the Vicariate of Rome, even for those already licensed in another diocese, to ensure the candidate had the knowledge needed for such a delicate ministry. He passed to the full satisfaction of the examiners, who exempted Clausi from the two further examinations usually required.42

The sacramental ministry of confession was the new Minim father from Calabria’s first apostolate in time43 and would remain so in importance; it was also the first testing ground of his priestly zeal. Many came to him for this ministry and he welcomed them all, behaving “with such gentleness and charity and with such abundant light received from God” that his fame spread and he became “the admiration of Rome”.44

“By his manner he seemed a Saint Francis de Sales,” the priest Felice De Gennaro would testify, “and because of this gentle way of acting others too, as I heard, thought of him as being like that Saint.”45

But we know more. According to Fr. Carlo M. Orlandi, Fr. Bernardo received the penitent with great charity and gentleness, encouraged him to trust, instructed him in doctrine neither rigid nor lax but sound and discreet, and helped him confess, but prudently, not interrupting him while he accused himself except to remind him of the main headings. He kept the appropriate admonition for the end. Then with a few burning words he moved him to contrition and gave remedies and penance well suited to and opposing the vices to be corrected. Before giving absolution he first moved him to faith, having him repeat short acts of the Christian virtues.46

“Often he is the first to name the penitent’s faults, and very often, when the confession is over and he has asked the penitent whether there is anything else and received the answer, he goes on: ‘But why don’t you confess such and such a sin?’ And then he reveals to him perfectly the true state of his soul.”47

From others we learn:

“He never used the phrase ‘Ask God’s forgiveness’, but said instead: ‘Let us ask God’s forgiveness. Peccavi, Domine, miserere mei’ and the like, thus putting himself in the same position as the penitent.”48

He himself brought the same humility and compunction to his own confessions, kneeling and beating his breast, and each confession of his was a general confession, with great self-reproach and humiliation.49

It is also known that he was generally brief in confession, especially with women.50

To sacramental confession Fr. Clausi added, when asked, the apostolate of counsel and the spiritual care of the sick. People of every class turned to him, and not only from the Monti district. He gave counsel in private talks or conferences;51 he went to the sick at once as soon as he was called.52 Someone who often accompanied him on these visits tells us that on the way to the sick Fr. Bernardo usually kept silent, absorbed and centered on God, so that when his companion sometimes asked him something he would answer only in a few clipped words, preferring to prepare his spirit for that holy work by prayer. As soon as he entered the sickroom he knelt down and prayed alone in devout recollection. Then he said some prayers with those present and blessed them. When he exhorted the sick, he moved and stirred both them and the others.53

But what really led people to seek his sacred ministry and active help were his fervent prayer and charitable intercession. He was recognized as a man of prayer, a priest zealous for the true good of souls, and this was shown not only by the public processions and prayers held during the conclave after the death of Pius VIII.54 Fr. Bernardo devoted long hours of the day and night to prayer;55 he could be seen motionless in it, often invoking the Most Holy Trinity and the Blessed Virgin.

We know of his “extraordinary devotion” to the Trinity, which he often honored, frequently repeating the aspiration Tibi laus, tibi gloria, tibi triumphus, o Beata Trinitas.56 His filial devotion to the Virgin Mary, whom he called “Our Hope”, Mother of Grace and of divine Mercy,57 equally extraordinary, seemed to bring Saint Bernard’s back to life in him, so great were his love and trust in her.58 One day, taking out her image, he exclaimed with fervor:

“Here is my favorite; I have her engraved on my heart, and no human force can take her from me!”59

Before the Blessed Sacrament he prayed with ardor. He said the canonical hours with great attention and recollection, kneeling before Jesus in the Sacrament whenever he could.60 At Mass too he was so absorbed in what he was doing and so inflamed that he seemed rather an angel. Near the consecration he grew pale, but at Communion his face seemed to glow, and after receiving the Precious Blood he remained absorbed. He spent a long time in thanksgiving, prolonging it as much as he could.61

Together with prayer, penance, including physical asceticism, was the other factor in Clausi’s virtue, perfection and apostolate. Br. Lorenzo, whose cell was next to his, clearly heard at night the blows of the discipline with which he mortified his flesh and made expiation for his penitents.62
