Some asked Fr. Bernardo to be their spiritual guide, among them Giuseppe Capparoni, whose personal experience confirmed his conviction that he was dealing with a holy director, and who found his reputation less than his true merit.63 As the days went by, more and more people, including priests and religious, entrusted themselves to his spiritual direction.

Particular events then increased Clausi’s reputation for holiness and the crowds of devotees at the church and convent of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti: events supported by his outstanding virtue and priestly zeal and at the same time confirming them, since God worked them in his faithful minister as proof of his favor and of the mission he meant to entrust to him. In his humility God’s power of grace would shine.

On 2 February 1831, after fifty days of conclave and almost a hundred ballots, Cardinal Mauro Cappellari had just ascended the Chair of Peter and taken up the government of the Church, with the name Gregory XVI. He had been wished the virtues of his great immediate predecessors in the Roman Pontificate: faith, constancy, learning and fortitude.64 On 3 February, beginning in Bologna, uprisings broke out in various provinces of the Papal States, renewing the earlier revolts in Romagna and spreading like an oil slick to the Marches, Umbria and the Legations, where they joined the insurrection. If abuses, errors and incompetence were among the causes, it was stirred up by Carbonari, liberals and followers of Mazzini, encouraged by the explosion of nationalist liberalism that followed the new French Revolution of 1830 across Europe, especially in Poland, Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Switzerland.65 In Rome too the echo of the uprisings caused political unrest. The new Pope, physically unprepossessing but of extraordinary vigor, frank humanity and outstanding austerity of life, well versed in church matters, trained in ascetic spirit and zealous and hard-working for the Church, who as a cardinal had published “Il trionfo della Santa Sede e della Chiesa contro gli assalti dei novatori”,66 set about the reform of public administration that would give his new government a good start.67 At the same time, on the religious front, he called for public prayers for peace and order within the Church. Fr. Bernardo responded with the intensity and fervor that came from his faith and charity, as well as obedience to the Vicar of Christ, adding to prayer a personal offering of expiation for the Church, tried in the universal Shepherd and his flock. In this inner climate of intercessory service, passing one day by the church of Saints Quiricus and Julitta68 and going in as usual to pray for the Pope’s intentions before the image of the Most Holy Trinity crowning the Blessed Virgin, he received a message to pass on to the Holy Father; a voice:

The first to be surprised was Clausi himself, who confided to his confrere Fr. Luigi Martini:

“Thinking it was an illusion of my senses, though I was astonished, I left the church to continue on my way. But after a few steps outside the church I found myself surrounded as if by a high wall that would not let me go on. I was beside myself, and full of confusion, not knowing what to do, I went back into the church to continue praying; and a second time I heard, in a louder tone, the same voice saying to me as before: ‘Go to the Pope and tell him not to worry.’ My confusion grew still greater, unworthy as I am, thinking it was an illusion of my senses. I left the church again to go about my business, but after a few more steps outside I found myself surrounded again by the same wall. Utterly confused, I went back into the church to repeat my prayer, and then, in a louder tone than the other two times, I heard the same voice.”70

68 This church, then a Dominican parish and now a chapel of ease of the parish of Saints Cosmas and Damian, served by the Third Order Regular of Saint Francis of Assisi, stands behind Trajan’s Markets, a few steps from the Torre dei Conti and the Roman Forum, about four hundred meters from the church of Saint Francis of Paola.

So he decided to go to the Holy Father, and what a surprise awaited him!

“All at once I went to the Vatican. When I got there and asked for the Pope, the guards made many difficulties, but by God’s mercy, after insisting and pleading, I was granted an audience with the Pope. I threw myself at his feet and, as if a higher power were urging me to speak at that very moment, I said to the Pope: ‘Your Holiness, God sends me to Your Holiness to tell you not to worry, because the political unrest will soon die down and the Church will recover her peace.’”71

Gregory XVI listened to him, and together they knelt before the little picture of Our Lady (the “Madonnina”) that Fr. Bernardo set on his table, to thank her.72 Then, at Clausi’s request, the Pope graciously attached to the image the plenary indulgence “toties quoties”,73 not only for him but for all the Catholic faithful.

A first sign of this was that the Pope, in dismissing him, accompanied him to the door of the audience room. The astonishment of the antechamber staff and guards, who could hardly believe their eyes on seeing the man they had tried to keep out treated with reverence by the Pope, is easy to imagine.

Fr. Bernardo at once responded to the Pope’s kindness with gratitude. Happy at having fulfilled his mission and at the treasure of indulgence he carried with him, in the height of his simplicity and contentment, back at his convent he picked three oranges from Blessed Nicola’s tree and went back to the Pope to offer them to him. This time he met no obstacles, and he thanked him for the indulgences attached to the “Madonnina”.75 Admiration and esteem grew in the Pope’s heart for the virtue of this Minim religious, towards whom he would always show trust and veneration.

Meanwhile the political unrest calmed down, and Gregory XVI, who had already thought of withdrawing to the fortress of Castel Sant’Angelo, did not leave the Vatican. Not all the ferment died away, but calm, however precarious, returned and lasted through this pontificate and the first years of the next. On the evening of 25 May Clausi went to the Pope again, and to the question:

“What good news brings you here, Father Bernardo?” he replied: “Tomorrow all anguish and fear will be over; tomorrow [the feast of Saint Philip Neri] will be Your Holiness’s greatest triumph.”

This happened exactly at the Holy Father’s visit to the Chiesa Nuova.76 New centers of revolt would flare up here and there in the Papal States for political reasons and economic hardship, fanned by discontent with poor temporal administration, but Rome was spared throughout this period, despite the hostility to papal government that began immediately after the election and spread through all social classes.77

Clausi’s mission remained hidden until, some years later, he confided it to Fr. Martini, who kept asking him why the Pope held him in such great esteem and veneration.

He called the celebrant several times, “Father Bernardo! Father Bernardo!…”, and he, roused from his ecstasy, came down and continued the Mass. Afterwards, deeply embarrassed, he knelt at Don Terenzi’s feet and humbly begged him to excuse him and keep what had happened secret. Then he took a hasty and somewhat crestfallen leave of Sr. Luisa’s sisters, who had also watched from the choir lofts, and went back to his convent at Monti. That same day, contrary to Clausi’s request, news of the ecstasy went round Rome and reached the Cardinal Vicar, Placido Zurla, who was at the Perpetual Adorers for a religious ceremony. Without delay His Eminence went to the Minim nuns’ monastery to verify the fact.80

Spreading rapidly, it was on everyone’s lips. People talked of it in families and religious communities, and many went to the Minims’ convent to see the

“holy” father, to entrust him with a prayer intention, ask his advice or bring him the sick and suffering for his blessing and intercession. Among other cases, two were brought to him that were attributed to spells cast by neighbors. They concerned two girls, Maria, daughter of one Giovanna Andreozzi, and her friend Maria Angela, both possessed by an evil spirit.81 Doctors and exorcisms had already been tried in vain.

The first, after much reluctance and backtracking, was persuaded by her mother to go with her to Fr. Bernardo; the other followed her example and invitation. Only a few days had passed since the Father’s public ecstasy, and devotees and the curious were crowding the church of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti and the little square in front. Maria arrived with her mother, and Maria Angela too. They had already noticed some relief from the blessing with the Father’s cord; he was not in the convent at the moment but arrived shortly after. He found the two young women, who meanwhile had had a new fit, threatening to strangle each other and barely held back and kept apart by those present, and turning to the first he addressed the demon oppressing her:

“Did you think, you ugly demon, that you would drink rosolio today as you drank it yesterday? I command you in the name of God to leave this body free!”

At this command Maria was freed from the evil spirit and fell on her knees before Fr. Bernardo. But he told her to get up, took her into the church before the image of the Immaculate and added:

“Now you are healed; forgive whoever did you this harm.82 Go and thank Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament and ask him for the grace you desire.”

He did the same with Maria Angela.83 Those present could not help crying “miracle”, and then they witnessed another.

Outside in the square a lawyer known to be ill was waiting in a carriage; drawn by Clausi’s reputation for holiness, he had come to ask for his blessing. Paralyzed, he could not get down, and sent his servant to beg the good Father to come to him. Fr. Bernardo went at once and, quite naturally, taking the sick man by the arm, invited him to get down and come into the church: “Come with me.” The lawyer obeyed and went home healed, and together they thanked the Lord for the favor received. The admiration of those present knew no bounds.84

We realize that Clausi was aware of the extraordinary charisms God gave him for the benefit and service of the people, and that he also understood the danger to which their publicity exposed his virtue; so he used every means to guard it and keep himself in holy humility. For this purpose he would use his own cheerful nature, his simple manners, the customs of his homeland and apparent eccentricities to divert all attention and curiosity from himself, though spiritual people recognized these as defenses of virtue.

That he was aware of this we learn from the Jesuit Fr. Antonio Ciccolini,85 who heard directly from him that he had had very clear knowledge, for example,

“of the state of people’s consciences: their thoughts, dispositions and sins were as if visible to his eyes”, “of having habitually felt in himself the power to persuade them, move them and convert them”; “of having in fact worked miracles of every kind: cures of utterly hopeless illnesses, both for their benefit and to frighten them salutarily”; “of having felt and experienced a power to work any miracle, with a subjective certainty that what he willed would happen.”86

One can say that Jesus’ assurance:

“Truly I tell you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, is clearly reflected in Clausi’s actions, prompted by the liveliest faith and Gospel simplicity. Fr. Bernardo himself confirms this.

“See how good God is,” he confided one day to someone he directed spiritually. “He uses this poor ragamuffin and sinner to do great things. This morning I went to visit the Blessed Sacrament in the church of the Adorers. At the door there was a poor cripple walking on crutches. He asked me to pray for him; I commended him to the Lord, and when I came out I felt an urge to tell that man to get up and walk. I told him, and he got up and walked. So you see that the Lord who works miracles uses the lowliest means to make his glory shine all the more.”88

A brief interlude at Paola

It is “a known fact”, Canon Valletta would testify, that Fr. Bernardo’s arrival in Rome and what was seen or known of his virtues and priestly zeal, together with the extraordinary signs, brought about “such crowds at the convent of Saint Francis of Paola” that one could not get across the square or through the church.89 Everyone wanted to speak to him, everyone put their hope in him,

ÞVJ.L II, LJ.

and blessing them with the “Madonnina” he sent most of them away satisfied, keeping others for confession, private talks or visits to the sick. Of the sick it can be said that there was no sick person in Rome who did not wish to confess to him, receive his blessing or confide their troubles to him. The same can be said of prisoners, with whom he spent whole hours on his visits, reconciling and comforting them.

Although his fame and following sprang from outstanding virtue and special graces, apart from an attraction that came also from his face, “always cheerful and gentle, always eager to help others”90 (but that was only outward charm), the prelates of the Vicariate, in agreement with his religious superiors, thought it prudent to send Clausi back to Paola. Testing his self-denial and detachment, and at the same time protecting his humility from possible harm, was the sole purpose of the transfer.91 So the time came to leave again, but before leaving Rome Fr. Bernardo had a farewell audience with the Pope. Some confreres who accompanied him begged the Holy Father not to let him be sent away, but the Pope pointed out that he too had been a religious and that it was better to obey. He kept Fr. Bernardo in private audience for about half an hour, then dismissed him, accompanying him

So on 7 July 1831, only eight months after his arrival, Clausi prepared to leave. A great many came to say goodbye, sorry to lose an apostle burning with such virtue and zeal,93 but he comforted them and urged them to trust in God. As he left the convent he repeated the exhortation to his confreres, who were also sad to part with him, and told them he would soon be back among them.

He sent a similar assurance to the Augustinian nuns of the monastery of San Silvestro in Capite, who had waited in vain to speak to him.95 not without visible emotion, to the door of the antechamber. “You will see me again soon, and you yourselves will call me back,” he added.

On the journey to Paola, where they were overjoyed to have him back, Fr. Bernardo, though keeping stops to a minimum and arriving incognito and leaving secretly, was shown esteem and veneration. His return to retreat and recollection in prayer, helped by the solitude of Saint Francis’s places, especially outside pilgrimage hours, would certainly do him good. He went there as to a spa for the spirit.

Counting his first novitiate, this was Clausi’s third stay at Paola. It would not be long, for in September his return to Rome would be ordered; meanwhile expressions of gratitude reached him at the Sanctuary from Rome for another remarkable cure attributed to his intercession. It concerned Sr. Maria Beatrice of the Sacramentines or Perpetual Adorers,96 to whom on leaving Rome he had sent blessed bread and an image of Saint Francis of Paola, asking her community “to say three ‘Glory be’ to the Most Holy Trinity every day, for two particular graces, in spite of ‘Principino’”.97 But he at once disclaimed any credit, saying instead that everything was due to God’s goodness. We have proof of this in the first of his letters from the Paola Sanctuary that has come down to us, in which he turns the credit to the power of Saint Francis’s patronage and above all to God’s charity in answer to everyone’s prayers.

“With the greatest pleasure,” he wrote to the Director of the Sacramentines at Sant’Anna alle Quattro Fontane in Rome, “and with much consolation I learned of the miracle worked by our wonder-worker of Paola, my holy Father, for the devout

Let us not cease, then, to pray continually to the Lord God, One and Three, that he may deign to hear us in everything according to his divine will and for his greater glory…”98

What Fr. Bernardo devoted himself to during this new short stay at Paola is quickly told. Church and choir, the “desert” and his cell were the places of his consecrated day, with constant prayer, religious observance and active priestly apostolate, as before. But the surroundings of Paola also asked to benefit from his devotion, charity and zeal, so there were celebrations and spiritual ministry in the neighboring villages and towns: Sotterra, Scarcelli, Fuscaldo, San Lucido. If the day was too short, filled with these works and ministries, he extended it with prayer at night, so that his spirit lacked nothing and he could respond generously to the needs of others.

The liturgical feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, Patron of the Order of Minims, on 29 September, is also traditionally, by Rule, the date of elective Chapters in the convents. At the Monti convent in Rome a new local superior had to be elected. The community was made up of members of the Mother Province, and its history and rights were tied to Calabria Citra, the Cosenza area, especially Paola. Religious were often exchanged between the Sanctuary community and that of the “College of the Calabrians” in Rome. Everyone there knew Fr. Bernardo and had heard of the latest miraculous intercession, which had occurred only a few days after his departure, following his suggestions. Above all, his virtue and example made them miss him. The Vicar General himself, Fr. Marsicani, who on his last “visitation” to Monti on 23 May had found “no serious faults”, finding in fact “prudence and vigilance in the superior, docility and obedience in the subjects”, anxious that the community should continue to give excellent edification and observance as throughout its two-hundred-year history, proposed Clausi’s candidacy in chapter. The capitulars were enthusiastic and unanimous, and the secret ballot produced a single name: Fr. Bernardo Clausi.

There was no difficulty about his return to Rome. Cardinal Zurla had personally checked the events attributed to Clausi’s miraculous intercession, including the most recent one in his absence, and was convinced. Confirmations of his uncommon virtue and merit also reached him.101 If anything, to prevent excessive esteem and spontaneous ovations, his outings from the convent would be limited and regulated so that crowds would not gather around him in the street. The Order’s superiors agreed, and his obedience for Rome-Monti was sent. Fr. Bernardo, embarrassed at the news of his transfer following his election as superior, adored the designs of God who was leading him back there. So he returned, traveling incognito; but the precautions taken to avoid popular demonstrations of esteem, homage and veneration were useless. Conscious of his own nothingness, however, he did not suffer from it. Applause embarrassed and humbled him, and he referred it all to the Lord: “Tibi gloria; mihi confusio” (To you the glory, to me the shame).102

“I have read the lives of many Saints who were humble and meek,” Arduini would declare, “but I have had to conclude that the Servant of God is second to none in the practice of this virtue.”103

And Don Stefano Miotti would add:

“Anyone who did not know him and would like to picture him alive should look at the painting of Saint Francis of Paola in his church ai Monti; there he will find the true portrait of this son of his.”104

notes.clausi-en-s8-n10: GIOVANNI BATTISTA PIZZULLO (Regina c. 1534 – Rome, 20 August 1623) was the son of Francesco and Caterina Grilli. He received his early education from the Minims of his town, to whom he was always grateful, owing them his start and success in priestly life and ministry (cf. TACCONE-GALLUCCI, Monografia, p. 13; PATRICCIOLI, Una istituzione calabrese, p. 9).
notes.clausi-en-s8-n16: Pizzullo paid 12,500 Roman scudi for the palace, tower, ball court and three gardens with their appurtenances. He took possession on 20 February, and only two days later it passed by gift to the Minims, by a deed approved by Gregory XV on 8 June 1623 (cf. PATRICCIOLI, Una istituzione calabrese, pp. 15-16). “Palatium cum illius mansionibus membris,” the document reads, “et pertinentiis universis situm Romae in Regione Montium, in Platea Sancti Petri ad Vincula, per ipsum ultimo loco et sub die 4 praesentis mensis emptum ab Illustriss. et Excellentiss. D. Joanne Georgio Duce Caesarino… cum omnibus viridariorum membris… ad haben[dum] ibique templum, Monasterium sive Collegium aedificandum, et construendum… ob singularem suam erga praedictum sanctum Franciscum de Paula illiusque Minimorum nuncupatam Religionem observantiam et devotionem… Item quod in uno ex praedictis viridariis e conspectu sacri templi B. Mariae Montium construi, et aedificari possit et debeat novum templum vel Ecclesia sub invocatione Sancti Francisci de Paula, cum sacristia, et aliis commoditatibus necessariis arbitrio ipsius D. Donatoris, ubi cadaver suum reponi, et sepeliri debeat…” (Fatti e documenti, pp. 19-22).
notes.clausi-en-s8-n18: PATRICCIOLI, Una istituzione calabrese, pp. 16-17. The sale had been authorized by Gregory XV with the Brief “In supremo” of 5 Jan. 1622. In 1582 Gregory XIII had enlarged the parish by joining to it two small neighboring parishes, San Salvatore ad Tres Imagines (or of the Holy Trinity) and San Giovanni Carapullo. The parish of Saints Sergius and Bacchus passed to the Minims, who settled there with a community of religious from Regina and other places in Calabria Citra and provisionally opened a chapel in honor of Saint Francis of Paola. The names of the members of this first Minim community are known: Fr. Giovan Battista of S. Agata dell’Esaro (Vicar Corrector), Fr. Francesco of Spezzano (parish priest), and the other professed religious Br. Dionisio of Paola, Vincenzo of Cosenza, Lorenzo of Spezzano, Michele of Regina, Paolo of Ruito, Giovanni of Regina and Antonio of Morano. Once the new Calabrian community at Monti was established, the Minims of S. Andrea delle Fratte transferred the inheritance rights to it by deed of 11 Sept. 1623 (ibid., p. 17). By that deed the College of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti was also formally established (legally recognized by Urban VIII’s Motu proprio of 8 Dec. 1624, confirmed by Alexander VII on 6 Nov. 1660). 19 TACCONE-GALLUCCI, Monografia, p. 18.
notes.clausi-en-s8-n25: As early as 1623 the parish of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti had 418 houses, 770 families and about 6,000 souls. Its boundaries reached Vicolo di S. Vitale, the church of Saints Vincent and Anastasius, that of Saint Susanna (then a parish) and the Montecavallo district; nearer, towards the church of the Madonna dei Monti (with the church of S. Salvatore, formerly a parish, later the Catechumenate); towards San Martino ai Monti, facing the Monte della Purificazione, the rise to Saint Mary Major and as far as the Strada Felice; and towards Saint Mary Major as far as the church of Saint Praxedes (then a parish). To the south it reached the Colosseum. A very large area, though not densely populated at the time; by the end of the seventeenth century the number of souls had doubled (cf. TACCONE-GALLUCCI, Monografia, pp. 20, 36).

Meanwhile the Minims officiated in the nearby church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, which, once the church of Saint Francis of Paola was finished, they had to hand over with its adjoining buildings to the College of Basilian Monks of the Ruthenian rite. This church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus is still served today by Eastern Catholics of the Ruthenian rite, after a different arrangement during the war years 1940-1945 and after. In 1730, however, at the wish of Pope Clement XI [sic], the image of the “Madonna del Pascolo”, found in 1718 under the plaster of the wall next to the sacristy, was placed for veneration on the high altar. MDCCCXIX. The whole church was given a Marian character, its vault being decorated with a large fresco of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. It was restored several times, including the façade, especially in 1896 at the wish and expense of Pope Leo XIII, and in recent years it has been enriched with statues of Saints of the Christian East.
notes.clausi-en-s8-n23: PATRICCIOLI, Una istituzione calabrese, p. 26. Altars, decoration, chapels, the travertine facing of the façade and a marble floor replacing the original brick were added over time and completed in 1826 under Leo XII, as recorded on another plaque in the sanctuary of the high altar. The church’s double title is documented on the first [plaque]: to S. Maria degli Angeli and Saint Francis of Paola (cf. note 11 in this chapter). It is also expressed in sculpture in the Saint’s chapel, where above his altar, in the marble crowning, two Angels flank in veneration a medallion with a high relief of the Assumption. Both to complete the church and to decorate the chapels and for the monumental façade, since the available cash from the Pizzullo bequest had run out (the rest was inalienable, for the College), further large donations were awaited, to which various devotees of the Saint of Paola, especially Calabrians and Romans, contributed generously (cf. TACCONE-GALLUCCI, Monografia, pp. 14-15). Above all, between 1645 and 1650, Donna Olimpia Aldobrandini-Pamphili, Princess of Rossano, widow of Prince Paolo Borghese, contributed (cf. TACCONE-GALLUCCI, op. cit., p. 21). The Aldobrandini arms were placed on the capitals both inside the church and on the façade. A first restoration was carried out out of devotion by Abbot Giuseppe Pallamolla in 1673 (PATRICCIOLI, op. cit., p. 29).

notes.clausi-en-s8-n35: It is not easy for a hagiographer to present this charismatic side of Clausi to today’s hypercritical readers, rather skeptical about anything miraculous. One risks being taken for naïve and credulous, if not obscurantist, and being ridiculed along with one’s subject. Yet this is the truth unanimously attested by people above suspicion, most of them direct witnesses of the facts they testified to in formal canonical processes. To pass over it deliberately or water it down into vague general references to charisms would be to defraud the truth and mutilate the authentic portrait of the person whose story is being written. In Clausi’s case it must be said plainly that the miraculous is one of the components of his supernatural experience, not an artificial halo. And if a proper sense of proportion counsels restraint in presenting it, this is so as not to overshadow, smother or distort with a mass of extraordinary events the other truly essential element, his outstanding virtues. These, after all, at an eminent level, already contain a supernatural motive and power and are a superlative response to the Spirit’s initiative and the gift of his grace.

notes.clausi-en-s8-n101: Canon Giuseppe Canali, Secretary and later Vicegerent of the Vicariate of Rome and formerly Bishop of Ferentino, took it upon himself to test whether his holiness was genuine. He did so at the first opportunity by wounding his humility. The first time Fr. Bernardo came to the Vicariate office to ask for a permission, he received him rudely and humiliated him in public. “Who are you?” he asked brusquely. “I don’t know you.” Clausi humbly introduced himself as the new superior and rector of Saint Francis of Paola ai Monti. “My uncle, frowning even more,” the witness Don Vincenzo Cavazzi would testify, “went on: ‘What are you telling me? Certain faculties are given only to distinguished and well-known persons,’ and sent him away, calling him a fool, an idiot and the like.” Fr. Bernardo did not reply but accepted the insult as an admonition. Deeply humbled, he knelt, apologized and withdrew without any sign of resentment, as humble as when he had come. The next day, meeting him in the street, he greeted him as if nothing had ever happened between them. “I am convinced he is a Saint,” Canali would say of him (cf. “Positio s. V.”, Summ., pp. 399-400, § 3; pp. 412-413, § 45; p. 414, § 52).

V.”, Summ., p. 409, § 30). Everything in him was guided by it. He would not let people kiss his hand, and if they tried he offered the cord or the habit, diverting their homage and gratitude to the habit the Saint of Paola gave his religious (cf. ibid., p. 399, § 1). “If you knew me,” he would say to those who praised him, “you would stone me” (cf. ibid., p. 105, § 5). At Genzano, for example, on his first journey to Rome, when the crowd waited for him outside the church to approach him and kiss his hands or habit in veneration, he shrank back and said earnestly: “Take stones and stone me, for I am the greatest sinner that […]”.
notes.clausi-en-s7-n14: It was not until 1857 that the obligation to make temporary vows, at least three years before perpetual profession, was introduced. The vow of a Lenten way of life, typical of the Rule of the Minims, is added to the other three common to religious life; it expresses first of all a regime of conduct, and therefore of penitential asceticism, physical as well, which draws on the spirit and asceticism of the ancient Lent, for the sake of greater penance and a more austere discipline.
notes.clausi-en-s7-n17: A marble statue of St. Francis was placed at the City Gate, perhaps already in the first half of the sixteenth century, as a sign of devotion and gratitude on the part of the townspeople. Other monuments to the Saint are to be found in Paola: in front of the church of Our Lady of Sorrows, at the beginning of the road that leads to the Sanctuary; at the end of that road, on the spur overlooking the Belvedere esplanade and the avenue of the Sanctuary, at the point that marks the boundary of the d’Alessio family’s small farm. This property was bought back at his own expense by the monarch Ferdinand II of Bourbon, on the occasion of his first visit to the Sanctuary, and returned to the Minims as having belonged to the Saint’s family, to be jealously guarded. In perpetual remembrance of that paternal property of the Saint and of the king’s generous gesture, a stele of local stone was placed there, with a plaque bearing the following inscription: Locum hunc B. Francisci de Paula / quem olim iure suo haereditario / minimis suis ligaverat / sed temporum infelicitate / postea alienatum / Ferdinandus II Siciliae Rex aere suo redemit / tantique Patris filiis / vindicavit volens libens merito / V Non. Apr. MDCCCXLV. Recently a bronze monument was erected at the junction with the expressway.
notes.clausi-en-s7-n18: The first Paolan hermitage, of which traces and rooms remain in the “grottoes” and the “catechesis room” below, goes back to the first eremitical movement that developed around Francis d’Alessio (or of Paola), already around the middle of the fifteenth century. The formal oratory, with the first cenobium, corresponding roughly to part of the presbytery and to the Saint’s chapel in the present Basilica, received the approval of the Archbishop of Cosenza, Msgr. Pirro Caracciolo, together with that of the eremitical congregation (later the Order of Minims) by the Bull “Decet nos” of 30 November 1471. The Saint enlarged it, because of the growing number of hermits who followed him, together with the enlargement of the adjoining formal little convent. The church and convent buildings saw further development after the Saint’s death (1507), that is, between his canonization (1519) and the tenth General Chapter of the Order (the first held at Paola), celebrated on 1 May 1535; for the church, however, it was a matter of decoration, brought to light again in recent work restoring the original fifteenth-century structure in local Gothic style. Afterwards, following the serious damage caused by the Barbary raid of Rais Dragut and the sack of 2 July 1555, the Sanctuary (church and convent) needed considerable repairs, carried out promptly under the provincialate of Fr. Marcello Palmieri (1554-1557), and enlarged in 1567, thanks above all to the generous contribution of Donna Isabella of Toledo, daughter of the Viceroy of Naples, Don Pedro, and widow of Gian Battista Spinelli junior, lord of nearby Fuscaldo. In the middle of the seventeenth century the sacred buildings were given a new arrangement: the convent was enlarged with new buildings on both sides of the Isca, chiefly the work of Fr. Domenico Ciandella, a native of Paola; the church, following the taste of the time, had its interior completely covered with Baroque superstructures that hid its original style, now instead rediscovered and fully restored. Between the one and the other construction the monumental central façade of the Sanctuary was inserted, with a double atrium (lower and upper) and guesthouse. From the end of the eighteenth century – exactly from 1779 – dates the Library added to the so-called Fathers’ wing, with in its vault a large painting of Genesis (of 1781) illustrating the meeting of the Queen of Sheba with King Solomon.
notes.clausi-en-s7-n29: From Catona, near Reggio, St. Francis crossed to Sicily on his cloak. This is the famous miraculous crossing of the Strait, mentioned in the Calabrian Process for the Saint’s canonization.
notes.clausi-en-s3-n1: Giacomo d’Alessio, son of Bartolo (also called Bartolillo or Martolilla, and by his close friends “Salicone” because of his great height), and Vienna da Fuscaldo were the fortunate parents of Saint Francis of Paola. Born on 27 March 1416 (the year is historically established), he brought the luster of outstanding holiness not only to his family but to Paola and Calabria; he scattered virtues and miracles across the lands of the old kingdom of Naples, Italy and France, where he ended his days at Tours, aged ninety-one, on 2 April 1507. Meanwhile he had founded the threefold order of Minims and accomplished a many-sided charismatic mission. He was a hermit and ascetic of the perpetual Lent; a wayfarer of God, champion and apostle of social justice; adviser to kings and an incognito diplomat in a friar’s habit; above all he shone as the most humble, the penitent, the Saint of charity. Leo X canonized him only twelve years after his death (1 May 1519; Bull Excelsus Dominus); Pius XII proclaimed him Patron of all Seafarers of the Italian Nation (27 March 1943: Brief Quod Sanctorum patronatus); John XXIII made him principal Patron of the Ecclesiastical Region of Calabria (2 June 1962: Brief Lumen Calabriae).
notes.clausi-en-s3-n2: The annual pilgrimage no longer takes place, as the roads have become rather chaotic with traffic, and since the men are mostly abroad for work, the women do not leave the village without their husbands. VINCENZO PADULA, Persone in Calabria (ed. Carlo Muscetta), n. p. 1878, p. 272. This work, originally entitled “Stato delle persone in Calabria”, won a prize from the Accademia Pontaniana in 1856 and is an early survey, though without modern scientific criteria, of the Cosenza area of Calabria in the first half of the nineteenth century. It collects articles by the author published in the newspaper “Il Bruzio”, which ceased publication on 18 July 1865. It is the most serious and perceptive work of this priest-poet from Acri, of rather eccentric and often licentious temperament, a liberal-leaning journalist, who led an eventful life from 25 March 1819 to 1893. His restless character made him critical of everyone, sparing no one his barbs, from the Pope to the humblest priest and religious; not even ours, but these were promptly countered by the general esteem and reputation for holiness that defended his memory. Well known is the stanza Padula dedicated to Saint Francis of Paola in a moment of conscientious regret for his past:

Sugnu chjino de peccati / ’nzing’ a diri alli quazuni: / mi li pozza illu lavari / ccu’ tri grana de sapuni… / (op. cit., p. 11).
notes.clausi-en-s3-n12: Montalto Uffugo, so called from its commanding position on the highest hill in the area and because it is more exposed to the winds and cold of the Calabrian winter, lies above the western slope of the Crati Valley. It was an episcopal see and one of the three main domains of the Ruffo family. The then villages of San Vincenzo la Costa and San Sisto were subject to it. Under the Aragonese, as its population declined, it came ecclesiastically under the archiepiscopal see of Cosenza; civilly it was held by the Moncada family and later feudal lords (cf. GIOVANNI FIORE, Della Calabria illustrata, I, Naples 1691, bk. I, pt. II, p. 106). Among those who ruled Montalto was the well-known pious and generous Simone d’Alimena, son of Guglielmo and Tedesca Luciferi, one of the most faithful benefactors of Saint Francis of Paola (cf. GIUSEPPE ROBERTI, S. Francesco di Paola – Storia della sua vita, Rome 1963², pp. 28-29 etc., passim). Many of the letters supposedly written by the Saint to Alimena according to Preste, published in the Centuria of letters attributed to the Founder of the Minims (cf. FRANCESCO PRESTE, Centuria di lettere del glorioso Patriarca San Francesco di Paola, Rome 1655), are spurious. A critical study has yet to establish the authorship of some of them.

notes.clausi-en-s4-n1:
That Rogliano was the birthplace of our Clausi’s father is known from a letter of his to Cav. Ciancio, in which he calls it “the town of my late father” (APGM, Ven. Clausi, fasc. 5: Epistolario, Letter to Cav. Agazio Ciancio, 11 July 1846). The genealogy of the Clausi of Rogliano goes back several centuries. Research into the line of ancestry has produced no results, as the old parish archives of this Calabrian town were destroyed or scattered during earthquakes.

The Clausi family, or Clauso by corruption (cf. APSS, Liber baptizatorum, year 1779, pp. 15 and 18, where Clauso appears three times, though referring to Antonio Clausi and his relatives Michele and Maria Giuseppa or to his own son Gaetano Maria), is typically southern in origin. There are Clausis in Sicily, Calabria, Apulia and Campania, but most of all in Calabria: at San Sisto dei Valdesi, Montalto, Cosenza, Rogliano and elsewhere. Paola too had a Clausi, the lawyer Domenico, a relative of our Vincenzo Maria; there is a letter addressed to him dated 18 February 1846 (cf. APP, file Ven. Clausi). History records among the Clausis priests and magistrates, teachers and men of letters and respected public administrators, such as Tommaso Clausi of Rogliano († 1670), jurist at the Roman Archiginnasio; Vincenzo and Bruno Clausi, canons in Cosenza and Rome respectively; Professor and Rector Pietro Clausi, a former pupil of Genovesi; Arnaldo Clausi-Schettini, mayor of Cosenza (1869); and patriots too, such as Raffaele Clausi of Montalto and Luigi Clausi of San Sisto (cf. DAVIDE ANDREOTTI, Storia dei Cosentini, Naples 1869, I, preface and pp. 398-399; III [Naples 1874], pp. 66, 181, etc., passim). Later the surname moved with its bearers to other regions of Italy, such as Lazio and Piedmont, but above all abroad, especially to North America (Canada in particular). The last direct descendant of our Venerable’s family, his great-grandniece Maria Clausi, died at San Sisto on 7 Dec. 1974. In the village they remember her as “Zia Maria” (cf. “La voce del Santuario di Paola”, Jan.-Feb. 1976, nos. 1-2, p. 19).

notes.clausi-en-s4-n3: In either case he did not belong to the “white bread” people, that is, the rich; but though it was rye bread, he never went without bread, nor without a little wine, which his own field provided, convinced as he was of the local saying: “Whoever wants to eat bread and drink wine, let him sow wheat and plant vines.” Whatever went with the bread was supplied by the owner of the estate, for whom he worked.
notes.clausi-en-s4-n4: The Caracciolo of San Sisto, who still live in the mansion that, with the adjoining streets, bears their name, descend from that Marino Caracciolo, Marquis of Bucchianico and governor of Calabria, who was charged by the Viceroy Duke of Alcalá, Don Pedro Afán de Ribera, through Don Ascanio Caracciolo, with destroying the centers of Calabrian Waldensian heresy (for the Instructions issued on 28 May 1561 cf. RITACCA, San Sisto, pp. 188-192). They settled there after the Waldensians’ defeat.
notes.clausi-en-s4-n5: San Sisto now has about 600 inhabitants. Emigration for work to the Americas since the beginning of this century, especially to Canada and the United States, has greatly depopulated it. In Clausi’s time it was one of the hamlets of Montalto Uffugo. In 1855, when San Vincenzo la Costa broke away from Montalto to become a municipality in its own right, San Sisto was attached to it as a village, together with Gesuiti. Still today, apart from the interval of 1928-1936 when all these places were annexed to the large municipality of Montalto, San Sisto, as already said, belongs to the reconstituted municipality of San Vincenzo la Costa.

Vaccarizzo, a hamlet or district of Montalto like San Sisto, though poorer, lies on a slope, laid out much like the neighboring hamlets, between its two churches to the north and south of the village: the parish church, larger than that of San Sisto, and San Rocco. Sisto, this point in the Confraternity’s Rules is very significant. It reflects the insistence of the bishops of Cosenza after the Council of Trent, starting with Archbishop G. B. One of the charges made against the local clergy of the Catholic places where Waldensian propaganda had taken root was neglect of the teaching of Christian doctrine, parish priests and their substitutes being very often busy with anything but the careful care of the souls entrusted to them. Poverty and precarious economic conditions were also a significant cause. Worst of all, however, was the lack of vigilance on the part of bishops, some of whom did not reside in their dioceses, an evil common to many other dioceses at the time and one of the wounds of the Church. The Council of Trent remedied the serious consequences by decreeing the obligation of residence for Prelates and parish priests (cf. Canones et Decreta Sacrosancti oecumenici Concilii Tridentini: Decretum de Reformatione, approved in Session VI, ch. I-IV, and Decretum de Reformatione, approved in sess. XXIII, ch. notes.clausi-en-s5-n54:
It is worth reviewing the clergy of San Sisto and the surrounding area at that time. The abbey-parish of San Sisto, the parish of Saint Michael the Archangel, had an Abbot-Rector and several other priests who assisted in the care of souls in San Sisto and the neighboring places of Vaccarizzo, S. Maria della Castagna and Rende, plus one entrusted with keeping the parish registers and overseeing the four curates. At the time in question the Abbot-Rector was Rev. Don Vincenzo Stella, appointed on 16 September 1802 after the death of his predecessor Don Giuseppe Archiopoli, killed “ictibus gladii a sicariis in domo suae habitationis” (by sword blows from assassins in his own house), aged 82, on 25 November 1801 (cf. AAC, File “San Sisto”: Archiopoli’s death record). We do not know the reason for this violent death. It was presumably robbery or revenge, since parish priests were then required to supply lists of births for military conscription, as there were no civil registers, and this was resented by draft evaders who took to the hills. There was also anti-clerical propaganda from extremists in various anti-government and anti-clerical movements, as well as politicized banditry (cf. RITACCA, San Sisto d. V., p. 153). Abbot Stella in turn died on the morning of 11 July 1818 (cf. AAC, File “San Sisto”; Notamento de’ Sacerdoti secolari che pretendono l’Abbazia di S. Sisto – copy made “ad hoc”). The new candidate for the office and title, and for the abbatial prebend of San Sisto and Vaccarizzo, was the priest Don Alberto Marimonte of Montalto, curate-administrator and primary school teacher in Vaccarizzo for eight years; but he was only interim Vice-Abbot, from 24 May 1822 to August 1825, since the then archbishop, Mgr. Domenico Narni-Mancinelli, informed him that he could not confer the benefice on him because he lacked the necessary requirements, although he had been presented by the Duke of Ferrandina and Montalto, who held the “jus patronatus” (cf. ibid., Letter of 26 Feb. 1824). On 20 August 1825 the same archbishop appointed Rev. Don Giovanni Carelli of San Fili Abbot-Rector (cf. ibid., Letter of Canon Chancellor Manfredi). Meanwhile, in August 1816, the curate-administrator of San Sisto was Rev. Don Domenico Madrigano, while in 1818 Rev. Don Giuseppe Caracciolo was responsible for overseeing the four curates and keeping the parish registers. Don Giuseppe Mazzuca does not yet appear among the four curates in 1818 (cf. the cited “Notamento ecc.” in AAC, File “San Sisto”). Only from 25 October 1821 is his signature found at the foot of entries in the parish registers, with the title of curate-administrator (cf. APSS, Register of the Dead from 1815 [year 1821], p. 43), while occasionally, for some time before, either our Don Vincenzo Clausi or Don Antonio Sicilia appears as interim administrator (ibid., p. 42f.).

Don Mazzuca came from a family of “braccioli” or day laborers that had recently risen to the class of “gentiluomini” or “important ones”, and since there was plenty of clergy in Cellara, his home town, he had come to San Sisto and joined the local clergy. Clausi would always be grateful to him for being his teacher, acknowledging that he owed him all his spiritual progress (cf. “Positio s. V.”, Summ., p. 63, § 6).
